Compound.name: cob(II)alamin-[methionine synthase]
Comment: |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13| is a vitamin B12-dependent zinc metalloenzyme that catalyzes the transfer of a methyl group from |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N| to homocysteine. Methionine synthase is one of two eukaryotic enzymes that require a cobalamin prosthetic group for activity. Unlike the other enzyme (|FRAME: EC-5.4.99.2|), which requires adenosylcobalamin, the cobalamin cofactor of methionine synthase needs to be methylated. Upon the initial transfer of a cob(II)alamin cofactor from a |FRAME: CPD-20918|, it is methylated to the active methylcob(III)alamin form by |FRAME: EC-1.16.1.8|, which uses |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as the methyl donor. The methyl group is subsequently transferred to homocysteine to form methionine, leaving the cofactor briefly in a cob(I)alamin form, which is regenerated to the active methylcob(III)alamin form by a transfer of a methyl group from |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N "5-methyltetrahydrofolate"| 2407589. The enzyme becomes inactivated occasionally during its cycle by oxidation of Co(I) to Co(II). Reactivation by reductive methylation is catalysed by the enzyme itself, with S-adenosyl-L-methionine as the methyl donor and a reducing system. For the mammalian enzyme, the reducing system involves NADPH and |FRAME: EC-1.16.1.8|. In bacteria, the reducing agent is flavodoxin, and no further catalyst is needed (the flavodoxin is kept in the reduced state by NADPH and |FRAME: EC-1.18.1.2|). A histidine residue embedded in the canonical B 12 -binding DxHxxG motif in methionine synthase serves as the lower axial ligand to the cobalt, which is bound in the "base-off/His-on" state 7992050.

Compound.name: a 6-phosphogluco-amylopectin
Comment: This compound class represents the |FRAME: CPD-7043| component of native starch grains that are phosphorylated on the C6 hydroxyl group of one or more glucosyl residue in one or more of the alpha-glucan chains. This modification is likely to produce a transition state for starch where the |FRAME: CPD-7043| glucans are less ordered but still insoluble 19325165. Starch is a combination of two polymeric carbohydrates (polysaccharides) called |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses| and |FRAME: CPD-7043|. |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses| contains up to several thousand alpha-glucosyl units linked almost exclusively in linear alpha(1->4) linkages, with very few branches of alpha(1->6) linkages. In |FRAME: CPD-7043|, on the other hand, branching is common, and occurs approximately every 24-30 glucose monomer units. |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses alpha-amylose| accounts for 30% of starch, while |FRAME: CPD-7043| accounts for the other 70%.

Compound.name: a [glycerolipid]-dimorphecolate
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-8204 Dimorphecolate|, an unusual fatty acid derived from |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| by the concerted activity of two divergent desaturase enzymes, is the major fatty acid (more than 60%) found in seeds of |FRAME: TAX-13490| species 14718523. It has three unusual structural features: 1) a C-9 hydroxyl group 2) conjugated Δ10,Δ12 double bonds, and 3) two trans double bonds, rather than the much more common cis bonds. |FRAME: CPD-8204 Dimorphecolate| has potential value in industrial applications such as the manufacture of paints, inks, lubricants, plastics, and nylon. Like other polyunsaturated fatty acids, dimorphecolate is not found in the seeds in a free form, but as a CPD-17286.

Compound.name: a homopolymer macromolecule
Comment: A homopolymer macromolecule is a macromolecule derived from one type of monomer.

Compound.name: a siderophore-bound Fe(III)
Synonyms: an iron(III) chelate // an Fe 3+ -siderophore // a ferric-siderophore complex
Comment: This entry stands for siderophores-bound |FRAME: FE+3| cation(s). Siderophores are small, high-affinity iron chelating compounds secreted by microorganisms. Once outside the cell, siderophores bind |FRAME: FE+3| with high affinity, and the iron-siderophore complexes are imported back into the cell by active-transport mechanisms. Siderophores are very common in pathogenic bacteria, since iron in the host organism is usually tightly bound to proteins, resulting in an extremely low concentration of free iron in the blood. Most siderophores belong to one of three major groups: the |FRAME: Catecholate-siderophores "catechols"|, |FRAME: Hydroxamate-siderophores "hydroxamates"| and |FRAME: Thiazoline-siderophores "thiazolines"|. Some grasses are known to make siderophores as well. These |FRAME: Phytosiderophores "phytosiderophores"| are also known as mugineic acids.

Compound.name: a rhamnolipid
Comment: This class contains glycosides composed of one or two rhamnose moieties joined in an O -glycosidic linkage to a non-glycero lipid moiety. The rhamnose moieties are linked to each other through an alpha-1,2-glycosidic linkage. The lipid moiety is mainly two (sometimes one or three) beta-hydroxy fatty acid chains (represented here in part by R1 and R2) linked to each other through an ester bond between the beta-hydroxyl group of the chain distal to the glycosidic bond with the carboxyl group of the chain proximal to the glycosidic bond. The carboxyl group of the distal chain is usually free, but in a few cases it is esterified with a short alkyl group. The fatty acid chains may be saturated, mono-unsaturated, or poly-unsaturated and the chain length may vary from C 8 to C 16 . In rare cases the rhamnose 2-hydroxyl group distal to the glycosidic bond may be acylated with a long chain alkenoate |CITS: [16160828] [20336292]|.

Compound.name: a prostanoid
Comment: The term prostanoid is used to describe a subclass of |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids| that includes the |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins| and the |FRAME: Thromboxanes thromboxanes|. These lipid compounds are derived from the ω-6 essential fatty acid |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|. Every prostanoid contains 20 carbon atoms with an internal carbon ring structure.

Compound.name: an aggrecan cleavage product
Comment: Aggrecan is a proteoglycan, a core protein modified with carbohydrates. The human core protein, encoded by the gene ACAN, is very large (over 250 kDa). Along with Type-II collagen, aggrecan forms a major structural component of cartilage, particularly articular cartilage. Aggrecan consists of two globular structural domains at the N-terminal end and one globular domain at the C-terminal end, separated by a large domain heavily modified with glycosaminoglycans. The two main modifier moieties are themselves arranged into distinct regions, a |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| region and a |FRAME: KERATAN-6-SULFATE| region. Certain proteases such as EC 3.4.24.80 and EC 3.4.24.82 are able to cleave bonds in the interglobular domain of aggrecan.

Compound.name: fucose
Comment: Fucose is a hexose deoxy sugar. It received its name from the brown algae genus |FRAME: TAX-3011|, from which it was first decribed. The alga was named because of its dark redish color, as one of the meanings of the Latin word fucus is "red paint". Algae of the |FRAME: TAX-3009| order produce fucose-rich polysaccahrides known as |FRAME: Fucoidans fucoidans|. However, fucose is a common sugar, found in N -linked glycans on the mammalian, insect and plant cell surface, in many bacterial glycans, and in other biomolecules. Most of the fucose found in biology is in the |FRAME: L-fucoses "L conformation"|, and the use of |FRAME: D-Fucoses| is rather rare (for example in some |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolide glycosides"|).

Compound.name: a 2,3,4-saturated fatty acyl CoA
Comment: This class describes ACYL-COA that do not contain any double bonds in the 2, 3, and 4 positions. Acyl-CoAs are oxoacids that have been activated by |FRAME: CO-A|. They are often classified by the length of their acyl moiety. This class includes the following sub-classes: |FRAME: Short-Chain-234-Saturated-acyl-CoAs "Short-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chains shorter than 6 carbons"|. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-234-Saturated-acyl-CoAs "Medium-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 6-12 carbons"|. |FRAME: Long-Chain-234-Saturated-acyl-CoAs "Long-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Long-Chain-234-Saturated-Fatty-Acids "2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 13-22 carbons"|. |FRAME: Very-long-Chain-234-Saturated-acyl-CoAs "Very-long-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 23 carbons or longer"|.

Compound.name: a galactosaminoglycan
Comment: |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans Glycosaminoglycans| consist of hexosamine and either hexuronic acid or galactose units that are arranged in alternating unbranched sequence, and carry sulfate substituents in various positions. The common glycosaminoglycans include |FRAME: Galactosaminoglycans galactosaminoglycans| (|FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| and |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|) and |FRAME: Glucosaminoglycans glucosaminoglycans| (|FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate|, |FRAME: HEPARIN|, |FRAME: KERATAN-6-SULFATE| and |FRAME: Hyaluronan|).

Compound.name: a [glycerolipid]-stearate
Comment: Stearate is a saturated fatty acid that occurs in many animal and vegetable fats and oils. It is a large constituent in milk fats, lard, and cocoa and shea butters. The name comes from Greek for "hard fat", reflecting the fact that stearate forms a waxy solid 16477801. Stearate was first described by Michel Eugene Chevreul in 1823. In cells |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| is usually found in the form of |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs stearoyl-[acp]|, |FRAME: STEAROYL-COA| or |FRAME: Stearoyl-lipid "incorporated into lipids"|.

Compound.name: a [receptor protein] (L-serine/L-threonine) phosphate
Comment: This generic class describes either a phosphorylated |FRAME: SER| or phosphorylated |FRAME: THR| within a receptor protein. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, R = H, in the case of |FRAME: THR|, R = CH 3 .

Compound.name: monogalactosyldiacylglycerol-38:6
Comment: In this group of monogalactosyldiacylglycerols, the length of the two acyl chains, and the location and number of the double bonds varies. For each of the group members, the total number of carbon atoms in the two acyl chains adds up to 38, and the total number of double bonds in the two acyl groups adds up to 6.

Compound.name: a TAG(18:3/40:0)
Comment: This class of triacylglycerols contains three acyl chains formed by the esterification of glycerol with three fatty acids. The names of triacylglycerol compound classes provide information about the three acyl chains of each member of the class, using the nomenclature TAG(a:b/y:z) where "a" represents the number of carbons found in one acyl chain and "b" represents the number of desaturations present in chain "a" and where "y" represents the total number of carbons found in the other two acyl chains and "z" represents the total number of desaturations present in the two chains included in "y." Therefore, in this TAG(18:3/40:0) class of compounds, one acyl chain has 18 carbons and three double bonds. The other two acyl chains have a total of 40 carbons and zero double bonds. The attachment sites of the acyl chains at the R1 (sn-1), R2 (sn-2), or R3 (sn-3) position along the glyceryl backbone may vary among class members and cannot be inferred from their order in the compound class name. Additionally, the location and orientation of the double bonds in the unsaturated acyl chain(s) may vary among members of the class and are not specified by this notation.

Compound.name: a vitamin
Comment: A vitamin is an organic molecule (or a set of closely related molecules) that an organism requires in small quantities for the proper functioning of its metabolism, but is unable to synthesize de novo and thus must aquire in its diet. Most vitamins are not single molecules, but groups of related molecules called vitamers, which can be converted to each other by enzymes present in the organism. Compounds that are required in large quantity (e.g. essential amino acids) or compounds that are inorganic (i.e. minerals) are not considered vitamins. Vitamins have diverse biochemical functions (e.g. enzyme cofactors, regulators of growth and differentiation, hormones, etc).

Compound.name: a high-mannose N -linked glycoprotein
Comment: High-mannose glycans typically contain between five and nine mannose residues attached to a chitobiose (GlcNAc 2 ) core, which links the glycan to an |FRAME: ASN| residue of a protein.

Compound.name: a glycosyl compound
Comment: A glycosyl compound is a carbohydrate derivative arising formally from the elimination of water from a glycosidic hydroxy group and the attachment of the exposed carbon atom to an oxygen, carbon, nitrogen or sulfur atom of a second entity from which an H atom has been removed.

Compound.name: a 3-hydroxy fatty acyl-CoA
Comment: Fatty acyl-CoAs are |FRAME: ACYL-COA "acyl-CoAs"| derived from |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, |FRAME: Fatty-Alcohols alcohols|, and |FRAME: Fatty-Aldehydes aldehydes|, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Short-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Medium-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Long-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "fatty acids that have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: VERY-LONG-CHAIN-FATTY-ACYL-COA "Very-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Ultra-Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Ultra-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain"|.

Compound.name: a pyrimidine base
Comment: Nucleobases are the parts of nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) that are involved in pairing of the two strands. The primary nucleobases are |FRAME: CYTOSINE|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: ADENINE| (found in both DNA and RNA), |FRAME: THYMINE| (found only in DNA) and |FRAME: URACIL| (found only in RNA), abbreviated as C, G, A, T, and U, respectively. There are many additional nucleobases, usually derived from the primary ones. Based on their structure, nucleobases are divided into |FRAME: Purines purines| and |FRAME: Pyrimidine-Bases pyrimidines|. |FRAME: PYRIMIDINE-RING Pyrimidine| is a heterocyclic aromatic compound similar to benzene, containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3 of the ring. The name pyrimidines is also used for compounds derived from the basic pyrimidine compound, including three of the bases found in nucleic acids, namely |FRAME: CYTOSINE|, THYMINE, and |FRAME: URACIL|.

Compound.name: monogalactosyldiacylglycerol-38:4
Comment: In this group of monogalactosyldiacylglycerols, the length of the two acyl chains, and the location and number of the double bonds varies. For each of the group members, the total number of carbon atoms in the two acyl chains adds up to 38, and the total number of double bonds in the two acyl groups adds up to 4.

Compound.name: an agarose
Comment: |FRAME: Agarans Agarans| and |FRAME: Agaroses agaroses| are sulfated polysaccharides that are extracted from sea weeds belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-2763| (red algae), mainly from |FRAME: TAX-2769|, and species from the |FRAME: TAX-31444| and |FRAME: TAX-33664| genera. The basic units of |FRAME: Agarans agarans| are repeats of beta -1,3 linked D-galactose and alpha-1,4- linked L-galactose units, which are substituted by sulfate. Different types of agarans have sulfate groups at different positions 1367970. In |FRAME: Agaroses agaroses| the alpha-1,4- linked galactose units are modified by having a 3,6-anhydro bridge. These bridges are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds, by forming a double helix during the process.

Compound.name: an olefin
Comment: This class includes hydrocarbons that have one or more carbon-carbon double bonds, not including formal double bonds in aromatic compounds. Members of this class may be cyclic or acyclic.

Compound.name: a pectin
Comment: |FRAME: Pectin "Pectin"| is a structural heteropolysaccharide consisting of a complex set of polysaccharides that is present in most primary cell walls and is particularly abundant in the non-woody parts of terrestrial plants. It is involved in crosslinking cellulose and hemicellulose fibers, which provides rigidity to the cell wall. The characteristic structure of pectin is a linear chain of alpha-(1-4)-linked |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| that forms the pectin-backbone, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl|. Diferent components of pectin have different substitutions and additions. A common type is |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan I"| (RG-I), which makes up 20-35% of pectin. In RG-I some of the |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| units in the backbone are replaced by (1-2)-linked |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, to which side chains of various neutral sugars branch off, mostly |FRAME: D-Galactose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-25028|. Another common type is |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan II"| (RG-II), which makes up about 10% of pectin. RG-II is based on a backbone of 8-9 galacturonate units, which are decorated by four side chains consisting of 12 different types of sugars in more than 20 different linkages. RG-II usually forms dimeric structures via the formation of crosslinks by a 1:2 borate diol ester between apiosyl residues in one of the side chains. Other types of pectin include chains of |FRAME: Apiogalacturonans apiogalacturonan|, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl homogalacturonan|, and |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan xylogalacturonan|. There is currently no consensus as to how the pectic polysaccharides are linked to each other, or to other polymers, in the wall. However, it is thought that the different peptides are covalently linked to each other via their backbones, forming a large linear structure with many side branches |CITS: [11423143][12162553][Coenen07]|. In nature, around 80% of the carboxyl groups of the galacturonate units are esterified with |FRAME: METOH|. Some plants, including sugar beet, potatoes and pears, contain pectins with acetylated galacturonate in addition to methyl esters. The salt of partially esterified pectins is called a pectinate, and if the degree of esterification is below 5%, |FRAME: PECTATE|. Pectin is used in the animal feed industry and in the food industry as a gelling agent. Phytopathogenic and saprophytic bacteria and fungi can produce variety of extracellular and intracellular enzymes that degrade pectin and its derivatives. Pectinolytic enzymes such as esterases, hydrolases and lyases, are used in the food, fiber and animal feed industries. There is commercial interest in pectinolytic enzymes to convert the pectin-rich by-products from citrus peel and sugar beet processing to higher value material. In 19618506 18535148 and reviewed in |CITS: [19159926] [REIGNAULT08] [8905080]|. Pectin structure is reviewed in 19616198.

Compound.name: a zealexin
Comment: |FRAME: Zealexins Zealexins| are a class of nonvolatile sesquiterpenoid defense compounds found in maize. They are produced in response to a wide variety of biotic threats, including TAX-5518 and other fungi as well as |FRAME: TAX-29057|. Jasmonic acid and ethylene can also work synergistically to promote zealexin production.

Compound.name: an electron-transfer quinone
Comment: This class holds |FRAME: Quinones quinones| that are involved in electron transfer within membranes. Quinones are organic compounds derived from aromatic compound, with two carbonyl groups incorporated into the ring structure with rearrangement of the double bonds where necessary. A classic example of a quinone is |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE|. Quinones are commonly named with a prefix that indicates the parent aromatic hydrocarbon (for example, "benzo-" for benzene, "naphtho-" for naphthalene, and "anthra-" for anthracene) with a "-quinone" suffix. Several types of quinones serve as electron acceptors in electron transport chains. Quinones can carry two electrons, and when fully reduced they are referred to as |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinols|. The addition of a single H atom to a quinone results in formation of a free radical called |FRAME: Semiquinones|. Many quinone derivatives often have other biological activities, such as |FRAME: CPD-11501 "vitamin K"|.

Compound.name: an oxidized flavin
Comment: A |FRAME: FLAVIN flavin| is a chemical moiety found in the compounds |FRAME: FAD| and |FRAME: FMN|, both important redox cofactors involved in many important reactions in metabolism. Flavin can exist in two different redox states, which it converts between by accepting or donating electrons. The |FRAME: Oxidized-Flavins "fully oxidized form"| (or quinone form) accepts two electrons and two protons to become the |FRAME: Reduced-Flavins "fully reduced form"| (hydroquinone form). The reduced form can be oxidized to a semireduced form (semiquinone) by donating one electron and one proton. A second oxidation results in restoring the initial quinone form. The conjugated ring system of fully oxidized flavin confers a bright yellow color, and its name is derived from flavus , Latin for yellow. Flavins are synthesized from |FRAME: GTP| in the form of |FRAME: RIBOFLAVIN|, which is later modified into |FRAME: FMN| or |FRAME: FAD|. Since mammals cannot synthesize |FRAME: RIBOFLAVIN|, it is an essential vitamin for them.

Compound.name: an N alpha -methyl L-amino acid
Comment: This compound class stands for generic and unspecified N alpha -methylated L-amino acids.

Compound.name: a deaminated amino group donor
Comment: |FRAME: Amine-Donors "An amino group donor"| is a compound that can donate an amino group to another compound in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes that belong to the |FRAME: EC-2.6.1 transaminase group"| (often called aminotransferases). Prior to donating the amino group the compound is |FRAME: Aminated-Amine-Donors| and after donating it the compound is |FRAME: Deaminated-Amine-Donors|. Since tranmination reactions are reversible, the distinction between an amino group donor and an amino group acceptor is not determined by the actual chemical entity, but by the role it plays in a particular reaction. However, some compounds, such as |FRAME: GLT| and |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, are often used as amino group donors by the aminotransferases in reactions that are physiologically unidirectional. This particular entry is used when the identity of the amino group donor (or acceptor) is not known or cannot be defined.

Compound.name: a campesteryl ester
Comment: This class of compounds includes campesteryl esters that have one acyl chain, denoted by R, connected to the campesteryl backbone via an ester linkage on the C3 carbon. For unsaturated acyl chains, the number, location, and orientation of the double bonds will vary between individual members of this group of compounds.

Compound.name: a (4 E ,8 Z )-4-sphinga-4,8-dienine ceramide
Comment: Ceramides are found in high concentrations within the cell membrane and are one of the component lipids that make up |FRAME: Sphingomyelins sphingomyelin|, one of the major lipids in the lipid bilayer. This type of ceramide, containing an additional double bond at position 8 of the sphingoid base, is a common modification in plants and fungi |CITS: [9786850][11171153][19047747]|. In plants, there is commonly a mixture of ceramides with the double bond at position 8 in both cis and trans configurations, whereas the double bond at the 4 position is generally in the trans configuration Lynch04. In the diatom |FRAME: TAX-35128| both bonds are in the trans configuration 15978045.

Compound.name: cellulose
Comment: Cellulose is the most common organic compound on Earth. It is a polysaccharide consisting of a linear chain of several hundred to over ten thousand beta(1->4) linked D-glucose units, and is the structural component of the primary cell wall of green plants, many forms of algae and the oomycetes. Cellulose is a straight chain polymer. Unlike |FRAME: Starch starch| or |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen|, there is no coiling or branching, and the molecule adopts an extended and stiff rod-like conformation. The multiple hydroxyl groups on the glucose moieties from one chain form hydrogen bonds with oxygen atoms on neighbor chains, holding the chains firmly together side-by-side and forming microfibrils with high tensile strength. Several different crystalline structures of cellulose are known, corresponding to the location of hydrogen bonds between and within strands. Known crystalline forms are named cellulose I, cellulose II, cellulose III and cellulose IV. Cellulose I is further divided into Ialpha and Ibeta, with the former formed by bacteria and algae and the latter by higher plants. Crystalline cellulose is not soluble. It is converted to a soluble, amorphus structure only at a temperature of 320 °C. Molecules with very small chain length, known as |FRAME: Cellodextrins cellodextrins|, are typically soluble in water and organic solvents.

Compound.name: [heparan sulfate]-alpha- N -acetyl-D-glucosamine 6- O -sulfate
Synonyms: a heparin N -acetyl-glucosamine 6- O -sulfate // [heparan sulfate] 6- O -sulfate
Comment: |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate "Heparan sulfate"| consists of a variably sulfated repeating disaccharide unit which is composed of a hexuronic acid and a hexosamine. The most common repeating unit, which makes up around 50% of the total disaccharide units in heparan sulfate, is composed of |FRAME: CPD-12521| linked to |FRAME: CPD-12541|. This compound stand for |FRAME: CPD-12541| sulfated at the C6 position within the context of |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate|, and not at the terminal non-reducing end..

Compound.name: a long-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acid
Comment: |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "A fatty acid"| is a carboxylic acid with a long unbranched aliphatic tail. This class describes |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"| that do not contain any double bonds in the 2, 3, and 4 positions. The compounds in this class are often classified by the length of their aliphatic chains. |FRAME: Short-Chain-234-Saturated-Fatty-Acids "Short-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids"| are 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chains of less than 6 carbons. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-234-Saturated-Fatty-Acids "Medium-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids"| are 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chain of 6-12 carbons. |FRAME: Long-Chain-234-Saturated-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids"| are 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 13-22 carbons. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-234-Saturated-FAs "Very-long-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids"| are 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 23 carbons or longer.

Compound.name: a carbobicyclic compound
Comment: Carbobicyclic compounds are bicyclic compound in which all the ring atoms are carbon.

Compound.name: topaquinone
Comment: Topaquinone (TPQ) is a ubiquitous quinone cofactor, existing in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic enzymes that include a divergent class of copper-containing amine oxidases. It is synthesized as a post-translational modification of a tyrosine residue within the polypeptide chain of the enzymes. TPQ is formed by self-processed oxidation of a specific |FRAME: TYR| residue in the presence of copper ion and molecular oxygen |CITS: [8082796][7798196][7718554][8798429][9047291][10074341][10736168][10736169][12134140]|.

Compound.name: a protopanaxadiol-type ginsenoside
Comment: |FRAME: Ginsenosides Ginsenosides| or panaxosides are a class of steroid glycosides and triterpene saponins found exclusively in the plant genus |FRAME: TAX-4053| (ginseng). They are the principal components responsible for the pharmaceutical activities of ginseng. Ginsenosides are composed of an aglycone and sugar moieties. Based on the structure of their aglycones, ginsenosides have been categorized into three broad types; |FRAME: Protopanaxadiol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxadiol-type ginsenosides"| (PPD), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 20, |FRAME: Protopanaxatriol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxatriol-type ginsenosides"| (PPT), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3, 6 and 20, and |FRAME: Oleanonic-acid-type-ginsenosides "oleanonic-acid-type saponins"|. Although ginsenosides only have three kinds of aglycones, more than 60 kinds of ginsenosides have been identified by now due to the variability in the type of sugar moieties, their number, and the carbon positions they link to. The biological activity of ginsenoside increases with the decrease of the number of the sugar moieties. All of the ginsenosides found in large quantities in wild ginseng (known as major ginsenosides) are heavily glycosylated, while the more active less-glycosylated ginsenosides are found in much smalller quantities (and are commonly referred to as the minor ginsenosides). Following oral intake of ginseng, the large low-solubility and poor-permeability major ginsenosides cannot be absorbed by the human body directly Su06, and are deglycosylated into smaller forms in the gastrointestinal tract by intestinal bacteria and/or digestive enzymes 8923812. Glycosidase enzymes that can convert the major ginsenosides to minor ginsenosides are not common and are of commercial interest.

Compound.name: an aldehyde
Comment: An aldehyde is an organic compound containing a formyl group (CHO). This functional group consists of a carbonyl centre bonded to hydrogen and an R group. Aldehydes differ from |FRAME: LONG-CHAIN-KETONE ketones| in that the carbonyl is placed at the end of a carbon skeleton rather than between two carbon atoms.

Compound.name: a sphingoid base
Synonyms: a sphingolipid long chain base // LCB
Comment: Sphingoids (sphingoid bases, or long chain bases) are building blocks of |FRAME: SPHINGOLIPIDS sphingolipids|. They are amino alcohols, composed predominantly (but not exclusively) of 18 carbon atoms. They are characterized by the presence of a hydroxyl group at C1 (and often also at C3), and an amine group at C2. The commonly known sphingoids include |FRAME: SPHINGOSINE|, |FRAME: D-erythro-Shinganines sphinganine| (dihydrosphingosine), and |FRAME: Phytosphingosines phytosphingosine| (4-hydroxysphinganine).

Compound.name: chondroitin sulfate A
Comment: |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates "Chondroitin sulfate"| is a sulfated |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| composed of alternating units of CPD-12557 and |FRAME: CPD-12521|. It is usually found attached to proteins as part of a proteoglycan. The saccharide units can be sulfated in variable positions and quantities - CPD-12557 can be sulfated at positions 4 and 6 to yield |FRAME: CPD-12516|, |FRAME: CPD-12565| or |FRAME: CPD-12526|, while |FRAME: CPD-12521| can be sulfated at position 2 to form |FRAME: CPD-12527|. The following names have been used to define different sulfation states: |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-A "Chondroitin sulfate A"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12516| |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-C "Chondroitin sulfate C"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12565| |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-D "Chondroitin sulfate D"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12527| and |FRAME: CPD-12565| |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-E "Chondroitin sulfate E"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12526| The term "chondroitin sulfate B" has been used in the past to refer to |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|, but is not used any more.

Compound.name: monogalactosyldiacylglycerol-34:6
Comment: In this group of monogalactosyldiacylglycerols, the length of the two acyl chains, and the location and number of the double bonds varies. For each of the group members, the total number of carbon atoms in the two acyl chains adds up to 34, and the total number of double bonds in the two acyl groups adds up to 6.

Compound.name: a fucan
Comment: Fucan is a generic term used to define a family of |FRAME: L-fucoses|-containing sulfated polysaccharides with extremely variable molecular weights that are produced by brown algae (|FRAME: TAX-2870|) Kylin13 and marine vertebrates Vasseur48. It has been recommended to use this term to refer to polysaccharide based mainly on sulfated L-fucose, with less than 10% other monosaccharides 12626402. In marine invertebrates, sulfated fucans have been found in the egg jelly coat of sea urchins |CITS: [Vasseur48][8071336]| and in the body wall of sea cucumber 3038547. In brown algae the fucan is present in the cell walls and can account for more than 40% of the dry weight of isolated cell walls Kloareg84. The fucans of brown algae are often called |FRAME: Fucoidans fucoidans|. The structures of fucans vary among species and sometimes among different parts of the organism Dietrich95. Fucan structures can be divided into three main groups: one group, found in |FRAME: TAX-33637| species of brown algae and several species of sea urchines, has a central chain composed of (1->3)-linked alpha-L-fucopyranose residues 8408031; a second group, found so far only in the sea urchins |FRAME: TAX-7640| and |FRAME: TAX-7671|, has a central chain composed of (1->4)-linked alpha-L-fucopyranose residues 11687579; the third group, which includes fucoidan isolated from |FRAME: TAX-52968| and |FRAME: TAX-3011| species of brown algae, has a central chain composed of repeating (1->3) and (1->4) linked alpha-L-fucopyranose residues |CITS: [11269406][21566795]|. Besides fucose and sulfate, the presence of monosaccharide residues such as mannose, galactose, glucose, xylose and uronic acids were also identified 18794778. Several fucose-containing polymers with less than 90% fucosyl residues have also been reported from brown algae and some of them were given names: ascophyllan or xylofucoglycuronan, isolated from |FRAME: TAX-52969|, is based on a backbone of mannuronate with branches of 3- O -D-xylosyl-L-fucose-4-sulfate |CITS: [Larsen66][Kloareg86]|; sargassan or glycuronofucoglycan, also isolated from |FRAME: TAX-52969|, is based on linear chains of D-galactose with branches of L-fucose-3-sulfate or occasionally uronate |CITS: [Percival68][Medcalf78][Kloareg86]|. However, those are classified as sub-types of fucoidan and not fucan, due to the large percentage of non-fucose saccharides.

Compound.name: a dimycocerosyl glycosyl phenolphthiocerol
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-18578 Phenolphthiocerol|-based glycolipids, known as PGLs, have been found in |FRAME: TAX-1769|, |FRAME: TAX-1768|, |FRAME: TAX-1765|, |FRAME: TAX-1781|, and |FRAME: TAX-78331| 3113946. The phenolphthiocerol moiety of PGLs is attached to mono-, tri-, or tetrasaccharide, depending on the mycobacterial species. Most sugar residues are O -methylated deoxysugars. The two secondary alcohol functions are esterified by |FRAME: Mycocerosic-Acids "mycocerosic acids"| or |FRAME: Phthioceranic-Acids "phthioceranic acids"|, depending on the species 3113946.

Compound.name: chitin
Comment: |FRAME: CHITIN Chitin| is a polymer of repeating units of beta-(1,4)-linked |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (GlcNAc) n . It may be the second most abundant biopolymer in the world, after cellulose. It is the main component of the cell walls of fungi, the exoskeletons of arthropods such as crustaceans and the insects, the radula of mollusks, and the beaks of the cephalopods. Chitin polymers have a high degree of polymerization and are insoluble in water 20559485.

Compound.name: alpha-amylose
Comment: |FRAME: Starch Starch| is a mixture of the two polymeric carbohydrates (polysaccharides) |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses| and |FRAME: CPD-7043|. |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses "alpha-Amylose"| contains up to several thousand glucosyl units linked almost exclusively in linear alpha(1->4) linkages, with very few branches of alpha(1->6) linkages. In |FRAME: CPD-7043|, on the other hand, branching is common, and occurs approximately every 24-30 glucose units. |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses "alpha-Amylose"| accounts for 30% of starch, while |FRAME: CPD-7043| accounts for the other 70%.

Compound.name: an iso -fatty acid
Comment: Iso-fatty acids are a class of branched-chain fatty acids (BCFA) that are characterized by a methyl-substituent located on the penultimate carbon of the carboxyalkyl chain.

Compound.name: Rhizobium leguminosarum bv. trifolii exopolysaccharide repeat unit
Comment: In nodule bacteria, the production of |FRAME: Exopolysaccharides exopolysacchrides| (EPS) is necessary for the nodulation of legumes such as Medicago, Pisum, Trifolium, Leucaena, and Vicia spp., which form indeterminate-type nodules. |FRAME: TAX-384| synthesizes an EPS that is necessary for establishing nitrogen-fixing symbiosis with Pisum sativum, Vicia faba, and Vicia sativa. This EPS is a polymer of a repeating unit consisting of a backbone of two glucose and two glucuronic acid residues, and a side chain that is biovar-specific. The repeat unit is modified by two pyruvyl and one acetyl substituents, and in some strain also by one nonstoichiometric hydroxybutanoyl group. The repeat units are linked together by an alpha(1->4) linkage. The structure shown here is from |FRAME: TAX-386| 29194398.

Compound.name: an aldose phosphate
Comment: An aldose is a monosaccharide that contains only one aldehyde group per molecule, located at a terminal carbon. It has the chemical formula H[CH(OH)]nC(=O)H, where n is equal or greater than 2. The definition of aldose also includes the intramolecular hemiacetals of such compounds.

Compound.name: xanthan
Comment: |FRAME: Xanthan Xanthan| is an exopolysaccharide produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-339| and related species. Because of its rheological properties, including high viscosity and pseudo-plasticity, and stability in extreme conditions, xanthan gum has been used in food, agriculture and industry as an emulsifying, thickening or suspending agent. It was approved for use in foods in 1968. Xanthan gum has been implicated as the pathogenic substance causing black rot in crucifers 9144435. The polymer is composed of repeating pentasaccharide units with the structure of a beta-1,4-linked D-glucose backbone with trisaccharide side chains composed of mannose-(beta-1,4)-glucuronic acid-(beta-1,2)-mannose attached to alternate glucose residues in the backbone by alpha-1,3 linkages 1212669. The terminal repeat unit is anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane by an undecaprenyldiphosphate lipid carrier, and assembley of the polymer occurs while anchored. Acetyl and pyruvyl residues are often added to one of the mannose units as non-carbohydrate decorations.

Compound.name: dermatan sulfate containing 4- O -sulfo- N -acetyl-D-galactosamine and L-iduronate 2- O -sulfate-[core protein]
Comment: |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate "Dermatan sulfate"| is a sulfated |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| composed of repeating disaccharide units of variable composition connected by a beta-(1->4) linkage. The dermatan polymer is attached to proteins via a linker region. Dermatan sulfate is expressed in many mammalian tissues and is the predominant glycan present in skin. Dermatan and dermatan sulfate proteoglycans have also been implicated in cardiovascular disease, tumorigenesis, infection, wound repair, and fibrosis 12213784. The most common disaccharide unit in dermatan sulfate is composed of |FRAME: CPD-12515| and CPD-12557, connected by a beta-(1->3) linkage. The two residues are often sulfated to |FRAME: CPD-12518|, |FRAME: CPD-12516|, |FRAME: CPD-12565| or |FRAME: CPD-12526|. Despite the fact that dermatan sulfate has been referred to as "chondroitin sulfate B", it differs from |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| by the presence of |FRAME: CPD-12515| (although some of the disaccharide units may contain |FRAME: CPD-12521| as in chondroitin sulfate) and is not classified as such any more.

Compound.name: laminaran
Comment: Laminaran (also known as laminarin) is a storage glucan produced by brown algae. It is a highly water soluble, branched polysaccharide based on a linear beta-(1->3)-linked glucose-based chain with an average degree of polymerization (DP) of 20-30 glucose units and beta-(1->6)-linked side chains consisting of one or more glucose residues. The ratio of beta(1->3) to beta(1->6) linkages is 3:1. Measurements conducted in 2019 along transects in the Arctic, Atlantic, and Pacific oceans revealed a median concentration of 26 +/- 17% laminarin within the particulate organic carbon pool 32170018.

Compound.name: an ω-hydroxy fatty acyl-CoA
Comment: An ω-hydroxy fatty acid is a fatty acid with a hydroxy group at the end of the chain that is farthest from the carboxylated end.

Compound.name: a {beta-D-GlcNAc-(1->2)-alpha-D-Man-(1->3)-[beta-D-GlcNAc-(1->2)-alpha-D-Man-(1->6)]-[beta-D-GlcNAc-(1->4)]-beta-D-Man-(1->4)-beta-D-GlcNAc-(1->4)-beta-D-GlcNAc}- N -Asn-[protein]
Comment: According to the nomenclature used for hybrid and complex N -glycans, this type of struc ture is known as bis-2,2. The term "bis" refers to structures with a bisecting N -acetylglucosaminyl (GlcNAc) residue, which is not attached to either the alpha-Man-(1->6)- or alpha-Man-(1->3)- arms of the three-mannose core, but directly to the mannosyl residue which is attached to the beta-GlcNAc-(1->4)-beta-GlcNAc-Asn-[protein] moiety. Bisecting residues are added by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.144|. The rest of the name is derived from having one N -acetylglucosaminyl residues attached by a beta1-2 linkage to the alpha-Man-(1->6) arm of the three mannose core, and one N -acetylglucosaminyl residue attached by a beta1-2 linkage to the alpha-Man-(1->3) arm 24178944.

Compound.name: a carbohydrate
Comment: An older definition of carbohydrates stated that they contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. As the term was originally applied only to monosaccharides, the name was formulated in recognition of the fact that their empirical composition can be expressed as C n (H 2 O) n . However, the term is now used in a much wider sense and includes |FRAME: Monosaccharides monosaccharides|, |FRAME: Disaccharides disaccharides|, |FRAME: Oligosaccharides oligosaccharides| and |FRAME: Polysaccharides polysaccharides| as well as substances derived from monosaccharides by reduction of the carbonyl group (|FRAME: Sugar-alcohols alditols|), by oxidation of one or more terminal groups to |FRAME: Carboxylates "carboxylic acids"|, or by replacement of one or more hydroxy group(s) by a hydrogen atom, an amino group, a sulfhydryl group or similar heteroatomic groups. It also includes oligo- and polysaccharides consisting of such modified monosaccharides, as well as derivatives of these compounds. An exception is |FRAME: Cyclitols cyclitols|, which are generally not regarded as carbohydrates.

Compound.name: a [(2,4),(2,4,6)]- N -linked glycan

Compound.name: a D- erythro sphinganine

Compound.name: a brassinosteroid
Comment: |FRAME: Brassinosteroids Brassinosteroid|s are steroidal phytohormones that regulate various important physiological and developmental processes, such as cell elongation and division, pollen fertility, photomorphogenesis, differentiation of vascular elements, and stress resistance |CITS: [16056912][Mandava88][15012241]|. Brassinosteroids, which have structural similarity to |FRAME: ECDYSONE|, the molting hormone of insects, are C 27 , C 28 and C 29 steroids depending on their C-24 alkyl substituents. More than 70 free, naturally occurring brassinosteroids have been identified in plants. The C 28 brassinosteroid |FRAME: CPD-697| (BL) is the most biologically active and together with its C 28 congeners is distributed widely in the plant kingdom 15012241.

Compound.name: a long-chain fatty acid
Comment: The term "fatty acid" was originally coined to describe aliphatic monocarboxylic acids derived from or contained in esterified form in an animal or vegetable fat, oil or wax. However, over the years the term has been expanded to refer to additional, shorter monocarboxylic acids with an aliphatic tail such as |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (but not the shorter |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: ACET|). The length of a fatty acid is determined by the length of the longest carbon chain, including the carbon of the carboxy group. Common natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbons in the longest chain and can be either saturated or unsaturated. In many organisms they are often modified by branching, hydroxylation, methylation, epoxidation and other types of modifications. Inside living cells fatty acids are rarely found in free form. They are usually bound to coenzyme A or acyl-carrier proteins, or form part of |FRAME: Triacylglycerides triglycerides|, |FRAME: Phospholipids phospholipids|, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|, and |FRAME: Cholesterol-esters cholesterol esters|. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, alcohols, and aldehydes, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "Short-chain fatty acids"| (SCFA) have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "Medium-chain fatty acids"| (MCFA) have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain fatty acids"| (LCFA) have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "Very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFA) have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "Ultra-long-chain fatty acids"| (ULCFA) have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain. Most of the natural fatty acids have an even number of carbon atoms, since their biosynthesis involves the addition of two-carbon-atom units. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. If it contains a double bond in the trans configuration, it is often referred to as a trans fatty acid. Most fatty acids in the trans configuration are not found in nature and are the result of human processing.

Compound.name: a hexose
Comment: Hexose is the name given to any six-carbon monosaccharide which in its linear form contains either an aldehyde group at position 1 (aldohexose) or a ketone group at position 2 (ketohexose).

Compound.name: an aromatic compound
Comment: An aromatic compound contains one or more aromatic rings (an aromatic ring is a planar ring in which every atom must have an occupied p orbital, which overlaps with p orbitals on either side). The pi orbitals of the ring's atoms form a conjugated system and are in resonance, giving increased stability compared to saturated compounds having a similar structure. As a result aromatic rings are very stable and do not break apart easily. The least complex aromatic hydrocarbon is benzene. The name stems from a time when compounds were characterized by their smell rather than their chemical structure. Similar structures in which at least one of the ring's carbon atoms is replaced by one of the heteroatoms oxygen, nitrogen, or sulfur, are called heteroarenes.

Compound.name: an H antigen
Synonyms: an alpha-L-fucosyl-(1->2)-beta-D-galactosyl-R // a glycoprotein-alpha-L-fucosyl-(1,2)-beta-D-galactose // a 2-O-(6-deoxy-alpha-L-galactopyranosyl)-beta-D-galactopyranosyl // an alpha-L-fucosyl-1,2-beta-D-galactoside // an alpha-L-fucosyl-1,2-beta-D-galactosyl-R
Comment: The |FRAME: H-antigen "H antigens"| are fucosylated oligosaccharides that decorate proteins on the surface of red blood cells in people with O blood type. In people with A or B blood types an additional monosaccharide is attached to one of the beta-D-galactosyl residues of the H antigen (|FRAME: CPD-12557| in |FRAME: A-antigen "A antigens"| and |FRAME: GALACTOSE| in |FRAME: B-antigen "B antigens"|). These fucosylated structures are found not only on blood cells but also on many other cell types (mainly epithehal), and it has been suggested that they should be called histo-blood group antigens. The majority of the A, B and H antigens are linked to the ends of long polylactosamine chains attached mainly to band 3 protein (encoded by SLC4A1), the anion exchange protein of the red blood cells. A minor fraction of the antigens is attached to a ceramide moiety, forming neutral glycosphingolipids. Several H antigens exist, differing in their core disaccharide 2093726. The different types are: |FRAME: Type-1-H-Antigen "Type 1"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-betaGlcNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-2-H-Antigen "Type 2"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->4)-betaGlcNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-3-H-Antigen "Type 3"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-alphaGalNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-4-H-Antigen "Type 4"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-betaGalNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-5-H-Antigen "Type 5"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-betaGal-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-6-H-Antigen "Type 6"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->4)-betaGlc-(1->R) Most of the H antigens found in the cell are either type 1 or type 2, followed by type 3 and 4. Type 1 is found in secretions and in the serum, while type 2 is found exclusively on the surface of red blood cells. Type 6 molecules have been described in exocrine secretions. It is not clear if type 5 H antigens exist, although the type 5 precursor has been characterized 2093726.

Compound.name: a type 3 histo-blood group antigen precursor disaccharide
Synonyms: beta-D-galactosyl-(1->3)- N -acetyl-alpha-D-galactosaminyl-R // beta-D-galactosyl-(1,3)- N -acetyl-alpha-D-galactosamine-R // betaGal-(1->3)-alphaGalNac-R // T-Antigen

Type 1 precursors are widely expressed on endodermally-derived tissues such as lining epithelia and glandular epithelia. Type 2 precursors are found mainly on ecto- or mesodermally-derived tissues, including erythrocytes Mollicone86. Type 3 and 4 precursors are found on ecto- or endodermally-derived tissues, including the salivary glands and kidneys 2464874. Compound.name: a phthiocerol B
Comment: |FRAME: Phthiocerols Phthiocerol|-based lipids and glycolipids have been found in many species of |FRAME: TAX-1762|, including |FRAME: TAX-1773|, |FRAME: TAX-1765|, |FRAME: TAX-33894|, |FRAME: TAX-1781|, |FRAME: TAX-1768|, |FRAME: TAX-1777|, |FRAME: TAX-1769| and |FRAME: TAX-1809| 3149973. Phthiocerols comprise a linear carbohydrate molecule to which one methoxyl group, one methyl group, and two secondary hydroxyl groups are attached. Two types of phthiocerols have been described. In |FRAME: Phthiocerol-A "phthiocerol A"| the methoxyl and methyl groups are attached at positions 3 and 4, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 9 and 11. In |FRAME: Phthiocerol-B "phthiocerol B"| a methyl group is missing from the beginning of the molecule, and thus the methoxyl and methyl groups are attached at positions 2 and 3, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 8 and 10. The two hydroxyl groups serve as attachment points for fatty acids, in a manner analogous to the much more ubiquitous sn -glycerol. The phthiocerol molecules have a range of 28 to 34 carbon atoms in the main chain, indicating a promiscuity of the enzymes involved in their biosynthesis. Longer molecules have additional carbon atoms added at the ω end of the molecule. In most organisms the two hydroxyl groups are esterified by |FRAME: Mycocerosic-Acids "mycocerosic acids"|. In |FRAME: TAX-1781| and |FRAME: TAX-1809|, however, they are esterified by |FRAME: Phthioceranic-Acids "phthioceranic acids"| |CITS: [3149973][3113946]|.

Four of the six coordination sites of the cobalt ion are provided by the corrin ring, while the other two are provided by |FRAME: Cobamide-Upper-Ligands upper| (beta) and |FRAME: Cobamide-Lower-Ligands lower| (alpha) ligands, which are located above and below the ring plane, respectively. Compound.name: a teichoic acid
Comment: Teichoic acids were first reported in 1958 Armstrong58, after being discovered serendipitously as "contaminants" in bacterial extracts from |FRAME: TAX-1590| 2662967. As they make up a significant portion of the cell walls (about 60% in |FRAME: TAX-1423|) 13684313, they were named based on the Greek word teikhos, which means a fortification wall. The teichoic acids are found in the cell walls of a wide range of Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [5411858][2496299]|. There are two main types of teichoic acids: the lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are anchored to the plasma membrane and extend from the cell surface into the peptidoglycan layer 406922, and the wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently attached to peptidoglycan and extend through and beyond the cell wall. In |FRAME: TAX-224308| the main form of teichoic acid is a polymer of |FRAME: CPD-75 "poly(glycerol phosphate)"|, while in |FRAME: TAX-655816| the major variety is a polymer of |FRAME: CPD-19310 "poly(ribitol phosphate)"| 13684313. In both cases, the repeating units are joined together by phosphodiester linkages, and are anchored via 2-3 glycerol phosphate units to a N -acetyl-beta-D-mannosaminyl-(1->4)- N -acetyl-alpha-D-glucosamine disaccharide. The glycerol and ribitol units of the polysaccharides are modified with D-alanine esters and/or monosaccharides such as glucose or N -acetylglucosamine |CITS: [13684313][4321415]|. It should be noted that strain 168 also possesses a |FRAME: CPD-19345 "minor form of wall teichoic acid"| that is comprised of poly(glucosyl N -acetylgalactosamine 1-phosphate) 4202940). Teichoic acids serve several roles in the cell. They serve as reservoirs of phosphates which can be mobilized when phosphate becomes limiting 104966. Being anionic, they are scavengers of cations (in particular Mg 2+ ), and may create a pH gradient across the wall by sequestering the protons expelled through the cytoplasmic membrane 8396121. In addition, lipoteichoic acids are the main source of the hydrophobicity of the cell envelope 6337099, and may contribute to its adhesiveness. Teichoic acids are also immunogenic, and can be considered the Gram-positive equivalent of the Gram-negative lipopolysaccharides 46620.

The functional group of lipoate is a ditholane ring, which is a cyclic disulfide. The enzyme complexes that require lipoate have a dedicated |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein "lipoyl domain"|, and lipoate is actually produced on this domain. The precursor |FRAME: CPD-195| molecule is first attached to a specific |FRAME: LYS| residue within the lipoyl domain (producing |FRAME: Octanoylated-domains|), and is then converted to lipoate by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-782|, resulting in |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein-N6-lipoyllysine|. |FRAME: CPLX0-782 "Lipoate synthase"| not only catalyzes the reaction, but is also the source of the two sulfur atoms.

Compound.name: NAD(P)H
Comment: |FRAME: NADH-P-OR-NOP| is a class of compounds including the instances |FRAME: NADH| and |FRAME: NADPH|. |FRAME: NAD-P-OR-NOP| is a class of compounds including the instances |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP|. |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| are dinucleotides containing one |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| base and one |FRAME: ADENINE| base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety. These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). They are often referred to as coenzymes, although in most of their reactions they function as cosubstrates rather than true coenzymes. The most common function of |FRAME: NAD| is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts |FRAME: NAD| to |FRAME: NADH|, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form. |FRAME: NADPH|, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of |FRAME: NADP|, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms |FRAME: NADP| is reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-84|. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY|).

Icosanoids participate in many cellular processes including promoting or inhibiting inflammation; responding to allergy, fever and other immune system challenges; regulating normal childbirth; contributing to the perception of pain; regulating cell growth; controlling blood pressure; and modulating the regional flow of blood to tissues. There are multiple subfamilies of icosanoids, the main of which are the |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins|, |FRAME: Thromboxanes thromboxanes|, |FRAME: Leukotrienes leukotrienes|, |FRAME: Lipoxins lipoxins|, |FRAME: Resolvins resolvins|, and |FRAME: Eoxins eoxins|. Each family can have up to 4 series of compounds, which are derived from the ω-3 fatty acid |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE|), the ω-6 fatty acids |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| [(5Z,8Z,11Z,14Z)-icosatetraenoate] and |FRAME: CPD-8120| [(8Z,11Z,14Z)-icosatrienoate], and the ω-9 fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-24529|, respectively.

Compound.name: a 1-phosphatidyl-1D-myo-inositol 5-phosphate
Comment: The phosphorylated derivatives of |FRAME: L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols "phosphatidylinositol"| (PtdIns), collectively called phosphoinositides (PIs), are eukaryotic cell membrane phospholipids whose inositol head group is phosphorylated at position D3, D4, or D5, singly or in all combinations, to yield seven PI metabolites. The seven phosphoinositides found in animals include: Phosphatidylinositol monophosphates: |FRAME: CPD-177|, |FRAME: CPD-1108| and |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-5-PHOSPHA|. Phosphatidylinositol bisphophosphates: |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-34-BISPH|, |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-35-BISPH|, and |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA|. Phosphatidylinositol trisphophosphate: |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL-345-TRIPHOSPHATE|. About phosphatidylinositol 5-phosphate (PI5P): PI5P represents only 0.5% of the PI pool present in most cells. However, its levels strongly fluctuate due to external stimuli such as TCR activation, insulin treatment, oxidative stress, and pathogen cellular invasion 28302928. Several studies found changes in intracellular PI5P levels during cell cycle progression, as well as upon thrombin treatment and osmotic stress |CITS: [10854858][11463365][11716778]|. The plant homeodomain-containing ING2 protein, a candidate tumor suppressor, was shown to act as a nuclear PI5P receptor, a function that regulates its ability to activate p53 12859901. PI5P has also been tied to tumor suppression via its potential regulation of Akt. It was demonstrated that the loss of PI5P, via a conversion to |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA|, resulted in a decrease in Akt activity 12897244. In addition, PI5P was shown to enhance the activity of various myotubularin phosphatases (MTM1, MTMR3, and MTMR6) toward their preferred substrate |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-35-BISPH|, presumably through allosteric regulation 12646134). Together these studies stress the importance of PI5P as a bona fide signaling molecule 15247229.

Despite its small size, it, is the most structurally complex pectin component. Its alpha-1,4-linked D-galacturonate backbone is decorated with four side branches (named A D) consisting of 12 different types of sugars in over 20 different linkages 18486536. Some of the sugars are quite rare, including |FRAME: CPD-13046|, |FRAME: CPD-20946| (3-C-carboxy-5-deoxy-L-xylose), and |FRAME: CPD-20949| (Dha). RG-II exists in the primary wall as a dimer that is cross linked by a 1:2 borate-diol diester 12226238. The borate diester cross link is formed between the apiosyl residue in side chain A of each monomer subunit |CITS: [8798473][10224062]|. Despite this complexity the structure of RG-II is largely conserved across plant species. It has been reported that the structure is virtually the same in members of the Brassicacea, Cucurbitaceae, Leguminoseae, Apiaceae, Liliaceae, Araceae, Amaryllidaceae, Gramineae, and more families 12765781. However, later work reported some variation in the side chains and methylation status within and across different plant speces 23802881. Please note that the structure shown here is not entirely accurate, due to the inability of software to depict unusual monosaccharides. |FRAME: CPD-13046|, |FRAME: CPD-20946| and |FRAME: CPD-20949| are depicted as generic pentose, hexuronate, and heptose, respectively.

Compound.name: a [cullin]- N 6 -[NEDD8-protein]-yl-L-lysine
Comment: |FRAME: Cullins Cullins| are a family of proteins that provide a scaffold for some RING-type E3 ubiquitin transferases (|FRAME: EC-2.3.2.27 "EC 2.3.2.27"|), which are not able to bind a substrate protein directly. These E3 proteins form a complex with a cullin protein and a substrate recognition subunit (SRS). Some complexes also include an adaptor that links the SRS to the complex. The complexes are known as CRLs for Cullin-RING ubiquitin Ligases. CRLs comprise the largest known category of ubiquitin ligases, and regulate an extensive number of dynamic cellular processes, including multiple aspects of the cell cycle, transcription, signal transduction, and development 18282298. There are five major types of cullins in metazoa, each of which forms a distinct class of CRL complex, with distinct adaptors and/or substrate-recognition subunits. CRLs are activated by the covalent attachment of the ubiquitin-like protein |FRAME: NEDD8 NEDD8| to the cullin, and are inhibited by binding to the CAND1 inhibitor 15688063. The human genome contains eight cullin genes.

Compound.name: a quinol

Comment: A quinol, or hydroquinone, is the fully reduced form of |FRAME: Quinones|. Quinones are organic compounds derived from aromatic compounds, with two carbonyl groups incorporated into the ring structure with rearrangement of the double bonds where necessary. Quinones are conjugated but not aromatic. A classic example of a quinone is |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE|. Quinones are commonly named with a prefix that indicates the parent aromatic hydrocarbon (for example, "benzo-" for benzene, "naphtho-" for naphthalene, and "anthra-" for anthracene) with a "-quinone" suffix. Several types of quinones serve as electron acceptors in electron transport chains. Quinones can carry two electrons, and when fully reduced they are referred to as |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinols|. The addition of a single H atom to a quinone results in formation of a free radical called |FRAME: Semiquinones|. Many quinone derivatives often have other biological activities, such as |FRAME: CPD-11501 "vitamin K"|.

Compound.name: a lipid-linked O antigen

Comment: O-antigens are part of |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|. Lipopolysaccharides are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides contain three parts: a lipid (|FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|), a |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, and polysaccharide side chains known as the O -antigen. The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of |FRAME: O-Antigen-Repeat-Units "repeating oligosaccharide subunits"| made up of two to eight sugar residues. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria 12007641. The presence or absence of O chains determines whether the LPS is considered smooth or rough, respectively. In addition, particular sugars in the structure, especially the terminal ones, confer immunological specificity of the O-antigen, in addition to the "smoothness" of the strain.

Comment: |FRAME: Carrageenans Carrageenans| and |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| are sulfated polysaccharides that are extracted from sea weeds belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-2763| (red algae), mainly from |FRAME: TAX-2769|, and species from the |FRAME: TAX-31444| and |FRAME: TAX-33664| genera. The basic units of |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenans| are repeats of alternating alpha-1,3-linked D-galactose and beta-1,4-linked D-galactose units, which are often substituted by sulfate. Carrageenans are classified according to the number and the position of sulfated ester 1367970. In |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units are modified by having a 3,6-anhydro bridge. These bridges, which form a double helix during aggregation, are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds. Despite this distinction, carrageenoses are often referred to as carrageenans. The three most industrially exploited carrageenans, namely, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan|, are distinguished by the presence of one, two or three ester-sulfate groups per repeating disaccharide unit respectively. |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan| is sulfated at position 2 of the beta-1,4 linked D-galactose units and positions 2 and 6 of the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units. Some carrabiose units of the λ-carrageenan from |FRAME: TAX-2765380| are substituted with four sulfate groups (D2S,6S-G2S,4S) 16716278. Since λ-carrageenans do not feature 3,6-anhydro-bridges, they do not make physical gels.

Comment: The term "fatty acid" was originally coined to describe aliphatic monocarboxylic acids derived from or contained in esterified form in an animal or vegetable fat, oil or wax. However, over the years the term has been expanded to refer to additional, shorter monocarboxylic acids with an aliphatic tail such as |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (but not the shorter |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: ACET|). The length of a fatty acid is determined by the length of the longest carbon chain, including the carbon of the carboxy group. Common natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbons in the longest chain and can be either saturated or unsaturated. In many organisms they are often modified by branching, hydroxylation, methylation, epoxidation and other types of modifications. Inside living cells fatty acids are rarely found in free form. They are usually bound to coenzyme A or acyl-carrier proteins, or form part of |FRAME: Triacylglycerides triglycerides|, |FRAME: Phospholipids phospholipids|, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|, and |FRAME: Cholesterol-esters cholesterol esters|. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, alcohols, and aldehydes, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "Short-chain fatty acids"| (SCFA) have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "Medium-chain fatty acids"| (MCFA) have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain fatty acids"| (LCFA) have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "Very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFA) have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "Ultra-long-chain fatty acids"| (ULCFA) have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain. Most of the natural fatty acids have an even number of carbon atoms, since their biosynthesis involves the addition of two-carbon-atom units. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. If it contains a double bond in the trans configuration, it is often referred to as a trans fatty acid. Most fatty acids in the trans configuration are not found in nature and are the result of human processing.

Compound.name: a ganglioside
Comment: |FRAME: Gangliosides "Gangliosides"| are molecules composed of |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids| (|FRAME: Ceramides| and |FRAME: Oligosaccharides|) with one or more sialic acids (usually |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|) linked to the sugar chain. They are components of the cell plasma membrane that modulates cell signal transduction events, and appear to concentrate in lipid rafts. The name ganglioside is derived from the ganglion cells of the brain, from which the first gangliosides were isolated by the German scientist Ernst Klenk in 1942 Klenk42. Indeed, gangliosides dominate the composition of the glycocalyces of most of the cells of the vertebrate nervous system. Although gangliosides with various glycan structures are found in every vertebrate tissue, they are markedly more abundant in the nervous system, where each cell has on average about 10 million cell surface gangliosides 27261254. Variations in the sialoglycan and lipid components of the gangliosides result in hundreds of distinct ganglioside structures with a variety of functions that ranges from regulating receptor tyrosine kinases to directing cell-cell communication, cell-substrate interaction, adhesion, and protein targeting 17991443. Mammalian brain gangliosides, however, are dominated by only four types of gangliosides - |FRAME: CPD-7188 "ganglioside GM1a|, |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINYL-ETCETERA-GLUCOSYLCERA "ganglioside GD1a"|, |FRAME: Ganglioside-GD1b "ganglioside GD1b"| and |FRAME: Ganglioside-GT1b "ganglioside GT1b"| 22735313. The ceramide lipid components of brain gangliosides are dominated by a single fatty acid (|FRAME: STEARIC_ACID|) attached to one of two sphingoid bases, |FRAME: SPHINGOSINE| and |FRAME: CPD-19684| 21113547. While many non-human mammals synthesize gangliosides that contain two types of sialic acids - |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| and |FRAME: CPD-273|, mammalian brain gangliosides almost exclusively carry the former. Like other glycosphingolipids, gangliosides are biosynthesized stepwise by a series of glycosyltransferases that use nucleotide sugar donors to first glucosylate ceramide and then elongate the saccharide chain .|FRAME: Lactosyl-Ceramides Lactosylceramide|, a product of the second glycosylation step in the biosynthesis of many glycosphingolipids, is an important branching point, being a common precursor for the synthesis of the four major classes of glycosphingolipids: the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|, the |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"|, the |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs "lacto series"|, and the |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs "neolacto series"| 10320813. The ceramide lipid of glycosphingolipids is embedded in the outer leaflet of the lipid bilayer of the plasma membrane, with the glycan extending 2-2.5 nm outward, perpendicular to the plane of the lipid bilayer 19056784. What makes gangliosides different from other glycosphingolipids is the incorporation of sialic acids. With a mean Pka value of around 2.6, sialic acids are more acidic than the majority of carboxylic acids and negatively charged at most physiological pH values. About the nomenclature of gangliosides Ganglioside naming is somewhat complex. Two ganglioside nomenclature systems are currently in use. The most commonly used is a short-hand nomenclature suggested by Svennerholm, which was initially based on the migration order of |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio-series"| gangliosides in chromatography 14066623. The more comprehensive system formulated by IUPAC 9826173 is applied much less frequently. A typical ganglioside name using the old system looks like |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"|. The first letter refers to the glycosphingolipid series. For example, the "G" stands for the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|. The next letter describes the number of sialic acid residues: (A = 0, M =1, D = 2, T = 3, Q = 4, P = 5, H = 6, S = 7). The following number describes the number of the non-sialic residues, and is derived in a rather complex manner. It was initially assumed that the number of such residues does not exceed 5. The number in the name was calculated as (5 - the number of uncharged carbohydrates). In addition, several sub-series of gangliosides have been defined based on the number of sialic acids attached to the galactose residue of the lacosylceramide core. If no sialic residues are present at that position, the compounds belong to the |FRAME: 0-Series-Ganglioside "0-series |. Those with one sialic acid at that position are named the |FRAME: A-Series-Gangliosides a-series |, those with two sialic acids belong to the |FRAME: B-Series-Gangliosides b-series |, and so on. |FRAME: C-Series-Gangliosides "C-series"| or higher gangliosides are rare in adult mammals and birds, but are abundant in fish and amphibians. Confusingly, GM1b and GD1c are both 0-series gangliosides, despite having a b and c in their names. So, for example, the |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"| is named as follows: G = belongs to the ganglio series, Q = 4 sialic acids, 1 = 4 non-sialic residues, and b = belongs to the b-series, meaning two of the sialic acids are attached to the inner galactose.

Compound.name: a pectate
Synonyms: poly(1,4-alpha-D-galacturonate)(n) // (1,4-alpha-D-D-galactosyluronate)n // 1,4-alpha-D-galacturonide // a pectic acid // an alpha-D-polygalacturonic acid // a poly(1,4-alpha-D-galacturonate)
Comment: |FRAME: Pectin "Pectin"| is a structural heteropolysaccharide consisting of a complex set of polysaccharides that is present in most primary cell walls and is particularly abundant in the non-woody parts of terrestrial plants. It s involved in crosslinking cellulose and hemicellulose fibers, which provides rigidity to the cell wall. The characteristic structure of pectin is a linear chain of alpha-(1-4)-linked |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| that forms the pectin-backbone, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl|. Different components of pectin have different substitutions and additions. A common type is |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan I"| (RG-I), which makes up 20-35% of pectin. In RG-I some of the |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| units in the backbone are replaced by (1-2)-linked |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, to which side chains of various neutral sugars branch off, mostly |FRAME: D-Galactose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-25028|. Another common type is |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan II"| (RG-II), which makes up about 10% of pectin. RG-II is based on a backbone of 8-9 galacturonate units, which are decorated by four side chains consisting of 12 different types of sugars in more than 20 different linkages. RG-II usually forms dimeric structures via the formation of crosslinks by a 1:2 borate diol ester between apiosyl residues in one of the side chains. Other types of pectin include chains of apiogalacturonan, homogalacturonan, and xylogalacturonan. There is currently no consensus as to how the pectic polysaccharides are linked to each other, or to other polymers, in the wall. However, it is thought that the different peptides are covalently linked to each other via their backbones, forming a large linear structure with many side branches |CITS: [11423143][12162553][Coenen07]|. In nature, around 80% of the carboxyl groups of the galacturonate units are esterified with |FRAME: METOH|. Some plants, including sugar beet, potatoes and pears, contain pectins with acetylated galacturonate in addition to methyl esters. Partially esterified pectins are often referred to as pectinate, and if the degree of esterification is below 5%, |FRAME: PECTATE|.

Almost all of the 2000 known members are derived from |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE|, which is biosynthesized from |FRAME: TRP| and |FRAME: SECOLOGANIN-CPD|. Though more than 42 skeletons have been described, they can be classified according to their carbon skeleton and biogenetic branch points into five major subgroups - the Aspidosperma, Ajmalan, Corynanthe, Iboga, and Quinoline alkaloids. Some of the MIAs exhibit a broad range of biological activities including anticancer, antimalarial, and antiarrhythmic properties.

To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Short-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Medium-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Long-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "fatty acids that have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: VERY-LONG-CHAIN-FATTY-ACYL-COA "Very-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Ultra-Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Ultra-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain"|.

They contain a six-membered heterocyclic, non-aromatic ring consisting of five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom and containing two double bonds and a ketone functional group. Most pyones belong to either of two isomers based on the |FRAME: CPD-11706| (2-pyrone) or |FRAME: CPD-26550| (4-pyrone) structure. The 2-pyrone structure common in nature as part of the |FRAME: Coumarins "coumarin"| ring system, while the 4-pyrone structure is found in some natural chemical compounds such as |FRAME: CPD-26551|, |FRAME: CPD-15508| and |FRAME: KOJIC-ACID|. 3-Pyrone structures exist, but are far less common.

The most relevant anteiso-fatty acids in food and bacteria are |FRAME: CPD-9917| and |FRAME: CPD-23509| 28129363. A distinct pre-dominance of ( S )- anteiso -fatty acids, or even ( S )-enantiopurity has been described in bacteria |CITS: [1886522][20117788]|, and also in fish |CITS: [13373794][17508720][20221853]|, dairy products |CITS: [13373794][13412644][13827622][20221853]|, mutton fat 13018208, and Brussel sprouts 26390192.
