Compound.name: a [cullin]-L-lysine
Comment: |FRAME: Cullins Cullins| are a family of proteins that provide a scaffold for some RING-type E3 ubiquitin transferases (|FRAME: EC-2.3.2.27 "EC 2.3.2.27"|), which are not able to bind a substrate protein directly. These E3 proteins form a complex with a cullin protein and a substrate recognition subunit (SRS). Some complexes also include an adaptor that links the SRS to the complex. The complexes are known as CRLs for Cullin-RING ubiquitin Ligases. CRLs comprise the largest known category of ubiquitin ligases, and regulate an extensive number of dynamic cellular processes, including multiple aspects of the cell cycle, transcription, signal transduction, and development 18282298. There are five major types of cullins in metazoa, each of which forms a distinct class of CRL complex, with distinct adaptors and/or substrate-recognition subunits. CRLs are activated by the covalent attachment of the ubiquitin-like protein |FRAME: NEDD8 NEDD8| to the cullin, and are inhibited by binding to the CAND1 inhibitor 15688063. The human genome contains eight cullin genes.

Compound.name: a strigolactone
Comment: Strigolactones are plant hormones that stimulate the branching and growth of symbiotic arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, but inhibit plant shoot branching. They promote the probability of establishment of a symbiotic association between the plant and the fungi. The first strigolactone (|FRAME: CPD-14655|) was described from |FRAME: TAX-3635| (cotton) infected by the root parasitic weeds |FRAME: TAX-4169| (witchweed) (hence the name). It has been shown that the seeds of the parasites germinated only if they were exposed to stimulant molecules present in the root exudate of the host. Although the nature of strigol was not understood at the time, it was observed that it was active at hormonal levels 17780042. Discovery of additional strigolactones from other plants followed, such as |FRAME: CPD-14659| from |FRAME: TAX-4558| Hauck92, |FRAME: CPD-14660| from |FRAME: TAX-3917| Mueler92 and |FRAME: CPD-14657| from |FRAME: TAX-57577| (red clover) Yokota98. The real purpose of strigolactones, which was understood 40 years after the discovery of strigol, is to promote the formation of symbiotic associations known as arbuscular mycorrhiza, which consist of close interaction between the plants roots and |FRAME: TAX-214504| fungi |CITS: [15944706][16574693]|. Arbuscular mycorrhiza, which are found in more than 80% of higher plant species, are one of the most ancient symbioses of land plants. The fungi acquire and deliver nutrients to the plants, which in return provides the fungi with carbohydrates produced by photosynthesis 15944687. The lactones induce extensive hyphal branching in germinating spores of the fungi, which increases the chance of contact with the root and subsequently infecting it. The branching phenomenon has been known for more than 30 years before the identity of the chemical signal that promotes it has been traced to strigolactone Mosse73. Since strigolactones are very labile and active at concentrations as low as picomolar, they are active only in close proximity to potential host roots, ensuring successful interactionbetween the fungi the roots. Study of mutants lacking strigolactones suggest that the hormones are also involved in the regulation of shoot branching, acting as branch-inhibiting hormones |CITS: [15268852][15342640]|.

Compound.name: a mono-rhamnolipid

The carboxyl group of the distal chain is usually free, but in a few cases it is esterified with a short alkyl group. The fatty acid chains may be saturated, mono-unsaturated, or poly-unsaturated and the chain length may vary from C 8 to C 16 . In rare cases the rhamnose 2-hydroxyl group distal to the glycosidic bond may be acylated with a long chain alkenoate. |CITS: [16160828] [20336292]|. Also see |FRAME: Di-Rhamnolipids| and |FRAME: 3-3-HAAs|.

Comment: |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids Glycosphingolipids| are a family of complex lipids composed of |FRAME: Ceramides| and mono- or oligosaccharide moieties that play an important role in various cellular functions including recognition, cell adhesion, proliferation and differentiation 8490246. Glycoshphingolipids have been classified into the following 12 series based on their structure: |FRAME: Arthro-Series-GSLs arthro|, |FRAME: Gala-Series-GSLs gala|, |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs ganglio|, |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs globo|, |FRAME: Isoglobo-Series-GSLs isoglobo|, |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs lacto|, |FRAME: Muco-Series-GSLs muco|, |FRAME: Mollu-Series-GSLs mollu|, |FRAME: Neogala-Series-GSLs neogala|, |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs neolacto|, |FRAME: Schisto-Series-GSLs schisto| and |FRAME: Spirometo-Series-GSLs spirometo| 25969757. Bile acids are classified into primary and secondary. The primary bile acids are produced in the liver from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|, while the secondary bile acids are produced by gut bacteria that modify the primary acids. About half of the cholesterol produced in the body is used for bile acid synthesis. The primary bile acids are conjugated in the liver with |FRAME: GLY| or |FRAME: TAURINE| before secretion into the bile. The natural forms of the vitamin are vitamin K 1 (|FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE|) and vitamin K 2 (|FRAME: Menaquinones|). Since menaquinones produced by different organisms have different tail lenghts, there are many variations of vitamin K 2 , usually specified based on the number of carbons in their tails, such as in Vitamin K 2 (45). Menaquinones are synthesized by gut bacteria, and are absorbed into the blood. Thus, dietary deficiency is extremely rare in healthy individuals. There are also several synthetic forms- vitamin K 3 through K 9 . Vitamin K 3 (|FRAME: CPD-3766|) is the most active of the synthetic forms.

Compound.name: a short chain fatty acid

Comment: The term "fatty acid" was originally coined to describe aliphatic monocarboxylic acids derived from or contained in esterified form in an animal or vegetable fat, oil or wax. However, over the years the term has been expanded to refer to additional, shorter monocarboxylic acids with an aliphatic tail such as |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (but not the shorter |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: ACET|). The length of a fatty acid is determined by the length of the longest carbon chain, including the carbon of the carboxy group. Common natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbons in the longest chain and can be either saturated or unsaturated. In many organisms they are often modified by branching, hydroxylation, methylation, epoxidation and other types of modifications. Inside living cells fatty acids are rarely found in free form. They are usually bound to coenzyme A or acyl-carrier proteins, or form part of |FRAME: Triacylglycerides triglycerides|, |FRAME: Phospholipids phospholipids|, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|, and |FRAME: Cholesterol-esters cholesterol esters|. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, alcohols, and aldehydes, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "Short-chain fatty acids"| (SCFA) have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "Medium-chain fatty acids"| (MCFA) have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain fatty acids"| (LCFA) have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "Very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFA) have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "Ultra-long-chain fatty acids"| (ULCFA) have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain. Most of the natural fatty acids have an even number of carbon atoms, since their biosynthesis involves the addition of two-carbon-atom units. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. If it contains a double bond in the trans configuration, it is often referred to as a trans fatty acid. Most fatty acids in the trans configuration are not found in nature and are the result of human processing.

Compound.name: a reduced two electron carrier
Synonyms: a reduced unknown two electron donor // A(H2) // a reduced unknown two electron acceptor
Comment: In general, an electron carrier is a chemical entity that can accept or donate electrons from/to another chemical entity. When accepting electrons, it acts as an "electron acceptor". By accepting the electrons, the acceptor is reduced, and thus prior to receiving the electrons the entity is called "an oxidized electron acceptor" and after receiving them it is called "a reduced electron acceptor". Many reduced electron acceptors are able to transfer the electrons to other molecules, becoming oxidized in the process. Thus the distinction between an electron acceptor and an electron donor is often not determined by the actual chemical entity, but by the role it plays in a particular reaction. However, some acceptors in biological reactions only accept electrons and do not transfer them further. Those are often known as "terminal electron acceptors". While in general every chemical reaction in which electrons are transferred includes an electron donor and an electron acceptor, several molecules are commonly used in metabolism solely for the purpose of electron transfer, and are referred to in biology as electron carriers. Different biological electron carriers differ in the number of electrons that they transfer and in their electron affinity. Some of the common biological electron carriers transfer only a single electron (e.g. |FRAME: Cytochromes cytochromes|, |FRAME: Blue-Copper-Proteins "blue copper proteins"|, and some |FRAME: Ferredoxins ferredoxins|), some transfer two electrons (e.g. some |FRAME: Ferredoxins ferredoxins|), some transfer a hydride ion ( e.g. |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP|), and some transfer two electrons and two protons (|FRAME: ETR-Quinones quinones|, |FRAME: FAD| and |FRAME: FMN|). In addition, a number of inorganic small molecules (e.g. oxygen, nitrate, iron (III), manganese (IV), sulfate) are often used as terminal electron acceptors. In many cases, purified enzymes can act in vitro using an artificial electron carrier, and their in vivo electron carrier is not known. The classes of "unknown electron carriers" are used to describe such reactions, which are incompletely characterized.

Compound.name: a cardiac glycoside
Comment: Cardiac glycosides are plant-made compounds (mostly by members of the |FRAME: TAX-4163| genus, or Foxgloves) that have beneficial effects over patients with cardiac failure. The treatment of congestive heart failure (dropsy), among other ailments like tuberculosis, by the use of Foxglove is mentioned in writings as early as 1250 A. D., when the Welsh Physicians of Myddva collected foxglove as one of their many herbs and included it in their remedies. 28561136. The cardiac glycosides are composed of two structural features: a sugar moiety that may contain one or more saccharides, and a steroid aglycone. Cardiac glycosides having a terminal glucose are called primary glycosides whereas those lacking such a sugar are termed secondary glycosides. There are two classes of cardiac glycosides differing by the group attached at the 17-position of the aglycone: the |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolides"|, which have a five-membered unsaturated lactone ring (but-2-en-4-olide ring) and the |FRAME: Bufadienolide-Glycosides bufadienolides|, which have a six membered doubly unsaturated lactone ring (penta-2,4-dien-5-olide ring). The steroid nucleus of the cardiac glycosides have a unique configuration: rings A/B and C/D are cis - fused while rings B/C are trans - fused. The nucleus has beta configured hydroxyls at the positions C-3 and C-14, and many compounds have additional hydroxyl groups at positions 12 and 16. The sugars found in the glycoside moiety range from common hexoses and pentoses (such as |FRAME: D-Glucose|, |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-Xylose|) to very uncommon sugars, some of which have only been found in cardiac glycosides (e.g. |FRAME: D-quinovopyranose|, |FRAME: CPD-22597|, |FRAME: D-Digitoxose|, |FRAME: CPD-22572|, |FRAME: D-Olivose|, and |FRAME: D-Fucoses|). While the mechanism whereby cardiac glycosides cause a positive inotropic effect and electrophysiologic changes of the hurt is still not completely clear, the most widely accepted mechanism involves the ability of cardiac glycosides to inhibit the membrane bound Na+/K+-ATPase pump responsible for Na+/K+ exchange KAUTE08.

These pathways converge at the compound Me-CoM, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|; the latter process involves methanofuran (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|). Compound.name: a menaquinol
Comment: Menaquinols are the reduced form of |FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinones"|. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are isoprenoid quinones of the naphthalene series, and are constituents of bacterial plasma membranes, where they play important roles in electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation. Menaquinones are the most widespread respiratory quinones in biological systems Fujimoto12. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are named MK- n or DMK- n , respectively, where the n refers to the number of prenyl units present in the side chain. The most common length of the side chain in bacteria is 8, although minor amounts of MK-1 through MK-14 have been found 7022156. Many bacteria and archaea have |FRAME: Dihydromenaquinones "dehydrogenated menaquinones"|, which are named MK- n (H 2 ). The degree and location of dehydrogenation depends on the species. Some organisms have menaquinones with modifications of the head group, for example |FRAME: TAX-2302| possess both |FRAME: CPD-15875 thermoplasmaquinones| (TPQ), which contains an extra methyl group, and |FRAME: CPD-15876 methionaquinones| (MTK), which contains a methylthio group 11157962. Menaquinones are also known as vitamin K 2 . Vitamin K is a name given to a group of derivatives of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone that are required by mammals for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, mostly involved in blood coagulation. These compounds, while essential for mammals, are not synthesized by them, and are thus considered vitamins. The natural forms of the vitamin are vitamin K 1 (|FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE|) and vitamin K 2 (|FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinone"|). Comment: |FRAME: CPD0-1099 "Colanic acid"| is an exopolysaccharide secreted by |FRAME: TAX-562| and a number of other |FRAME: TAX-543| that encapsulates the organism, resulting in a mucoid appearance 13963285. Colanic acid is thought to promote biofilm formation and to protect the organism when exposed to harsh environments such as acidic conditions |CITS: [11371548][16706906]|. Even though it wasn't identified as such, colanic acid was first described in 1927 by Dorothea Smith, who isolated a polysaccharide from a mucoid strain of |FRAME: TAX-562| 19869322. Fourteen years later, in a study on the antigens of the Enterobacteriaceae , it was noticed that one antigen was common to several mucoid strains of |FRAME: TAX-57045| Kauffmann41. It was soon reported that the same antigen, which was named "M" antigen, is produced by mucoid Escherichia coli strains 15406247. In 1954 Kauffmann reported that the antigen was common to all mucoid Salmonella species Kauffmann54. Similar exopolysaccharides were reported from a number of mucoid strains and species |CITS: [13475241][13641209][13963285][14073028][5324934]|. In the early 60s it was reported that a large number of Salmonella and Escherichia strains that are not normally mucoid can be induced to form slime exopolysaccharides when grown at 15 to 20°C in high phosphate concentration |CITS: [Anderson61][Anderson63]|, and the exopolysaccharide was named "colanic acid" after |FRAME: TAX-562| from which it was isolated 13963285. In a paper describing the discovery of the same polysaccharide in |FRAME: TAX-83333| it was suggested that colanic acid and the "M antigen" reported in the earlier studies are identical 14206589. A confirmation was obtained in 1969 when it was shown that colanic acid of identical composition is produced by strains from the genera Salmonella , Escherichia , and Aerobacter . At that time the exact structure was not known, though it was known that the polysaccharide contains glucose, galactose, fucose, and glucuronate, as well as some O -acetyl groups 4902806. Additional structural studies have shown that colanic acid from different organisms is very similar, with the polysaccharide composed of a hexasaccharide repeating unit consisting of glucose, two fucoses, two galactoses, and glucuronate. In addition, one fucose and one galactose may be acetylated to varying degrees, and the terminal galactose residue is modified. The repeat units are connected by a linkage between the first and third residues, with the remaining three residues forming a side chain |CITS: [4311825][4902692]|. Differences are found in the modifications of the terminal galactose residue, which was found to contain a 4,6-pyruvoyl group, a 3,4-pyruvoyl group, a 3,4-ethylidene group, or a 4,6-methylene group in different strains 4941627. The structure shown here was published in 2007, correcting several errors in earlier reports 17227761. While colanic acid was considered exclusively an exopolysaccharide that is only loosely associated with the cell surface, the 2007 study also found that colanic acid can be attached to the lipid A core of lipopolysaccharide instead of the O antigen, forming a novel type of lipopolysaccharide which was named |FRAME: CPD0-1101 M LPS | 17227761.

The physiological role of cyclopropane-containing fatty acyl chains (CFA) is to stabilize the membranes by increased ordering of the chains without sacrificing membrane fluidity. This can decrease the proton permeability of phospholipid bilayers, helping the bacteria survive acid shock |CITS: [9310851][18562182][25804677]|. trans -configured CFA in mycolic acids were reported to be correlated with the persistence of the pathogen and to modulate the innate immune response of the host 15710652. The basic units of |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenans| are repeats of alternating alpha-1,3-linked D-galactose and beta-1,4-linked D-galactose units, which are often substituted by sulfate. These bridges, which form a double helix during aggregation, are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds. Despite this distinction, carrageenoses are often referred to as carrageenans. The three most industrially exploited carrageenans, namely, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan|, are distinguished by the presence of one, two or three ester-sulfate groups per repeating disaccharide unit respectively.

Comment: The dissimilatory sulfite reductase, DsrAB, is an essential enzyme in prokaryotic sulfur-based energy metabolism. In sulfur reducers it catalyzes the reduction of sulfite to sulfide, while in sulfur oxidizers it catalyzes the opposite reaction Schedel79. This reaction involves the small protein DsrC, which is present in all organisms that contain DsrAB, including sulfate/sulfite reducing organisms, sulfur-oxidizing bacteria, and organosulfonate reducers. DsrC contains two redox-active conserved cysteines in a flexible C-terminal arm. A crystal structure of |FRAME: TAX-881| DsrAB in complex with DsrC has shown that the C-terminal arm of DsrC projects inside DsrAB in a way that brings its last Cys (CysA) right next to the active site. In the sulfur-oxidizing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1049| DsrC is the final sulfur-accepting protein, receiving the sulfur from the sulfur-carrier protein |FRAME: DsrE-Protein DsrE| and forming |FRAME: DsrC-persulfides "a perthiol on CysA"|. This perthiol is oxidized to form a trisulfide bridge with CysB. This trisulfide bridge then serves as a direct substrate for |FRAME: CPLX-7133| (DsrAB), which catalyzes an oxidation reaction. The oxidized middle sulfur is released in the form of sulfite, leaving DsrC with two reduced cysteine residues |CITS: [18656485][20952577]|. In sulfite reducers DsrAB catalyzes the opposite reaction, adding the sulfur atom of sulfite to DsrC and forming the trisulfide bridge with the two cysteine residues. This third sulfur atom is then released in the form of hydrogen sulfide in a reaction catalyzed by DsrK, restoring DsrC to its reduced form 26680199. In the structure shown below, the R residue represents a stretch of amino acids that separate the two conserved L-cysteines.

Comment: |FRAME: Ginsenosides Ginsenosides| or panaxosides are a class of steroid glycosides and triterpene saponins found exclusively in the plant genus |FRAME: TAX-4053| (ginseng). They are the principal components responsible for the pharmaceutical activities of ginseng. Ginsenosides are composed of an aglycone and sugar moieties. Based on the structure of their aglycones, ginsenosides have been categorized into three broad types; |FRAME: Protopanaxadiol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxadiol-type ginsenosides"| (PPD), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 20, |FRAME: Protopanaxatriol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxatriol-type ginsenosides"| (PPT), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3, 6 and 20, and |FRAME: Oleanonic-acid-type-ginsenosides "oleanonic-acid-type saponins"|. Although ginsenosides only have three kinds of aglycones, more than 60 kinds of ginsenosides have been identified by now due to the variability in the type of sugar moieties, their number, and the carbon positions they link to. The biological activity of ginsenoside increases with the decrease of the number of the sugar moieties. All of the ginsenosides found in large quantities in wild ginseng (known as major ginsenosides) are heavily glycosylated, while the more active less-glycosylated ginsenosides are found in much smalller quantities (and are commonly referred to as the minor ginsenosides). Following oral intake of ginseng, the large low-solubility and poor-permeability major ginsenosides cannot be absorbed by the human body directly Su06, and are deglycosylated into smaller forms in the gastrointestinal tract by intestinal bacteria and/or digestive enzymes 8923812. Glycosidase enzymes that can convert the major ginsenosides to minor ginsenosides are not common and are of commercial interest.

In bioluminescent systems, |FRAME: OPLOPHORUS-LUCIFERIN coelenterazine| is bound by either |FRAME: Coelenterazine-binding-proteins "coelenterazine-binding protein"| or by |FRAME: Aequorins "an aequorin"| protein, depending on the species. However, in vivo the excitation energy is transferred to |FRAME: GFP| by Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) |CITS: [4151620][33175]|. Coelenterazine is a derivative of imidazopyrazinone. Its biosynthetic origin is not known. However, it has been shown that the hydromedusa |FRAME: TAX-6100| is not able to synthesize it, and is dependent on a dietary supply of this luciferin for bioluminescence 11572972. The only report of de novo biosynthesis of coelenterazine is from the bioluminescent shrimp |FRAME: TAX-576189| Thomson95.

Comment: Glycosaminoglycans (also known as mucopolysaccharides) are important components of connective tissues. They are composed of long unbranched polysaccharides consisting of a repeating disaccharide unit. The repeating units consist of an N -acetyl-hexosamine and a hexose or hexuronic acid, either or both of which are often sulfated. Members of the glycosaminoglycan family vary in the type of hexosamine, hexose or hexuronic acid unit they contain (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-12521|, |FRAME: CPD-12515|, galactose, CPD-12557, |FRAME: CPD-12541|). With the exception of hyaluronan, the polysaccharide chains are linked covalently at the reducing end to a core protein through an O -glycosidic linkage to a serine residue. The modified proteins are known as |FRAME: Proteoglycans proteoglycans|. Most glycosaminoglycans are attached via a specific tetrasaccharide known as the |FRAME: GlcA-Gal-Gal-Xyl-Proteins "glycosaminoglycan-protein linkage region"|.

The biological activity of ginsenoside increases with the decrease of the number of the sugar moieties. Unlike cellulose, which is crystalline and resistant to hydrolysis, the other polymers are amorphous and are easily hydrolyzed by dilute acid or base. Hemicellulose is a heterogeneous term that is used for all the plant cell wall components that are soluble in dilute alkali solutions, or that go into solution quite readily in hot dilute mineral acids with the formation of simple sugars. The term is often used to describe all the polysaccharide components of the cell wall other than cellulose. Hemicelluloses constitute about one-fourth of perennial plants and about one-third of annual plants. Since the term does not refer to a particular chemical entity, hemicelluloses extracted from different plant sources are rarely identical. However, D-xylose is the dominant building unit of the hemicelluloses of most woods and annual plants. D-xylose occurs as the polymer |FRAME: Xylans|, as derivatives of xylan, such as |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans glucuronoxylan| and |FRAME: Arabinoxylan arabinoxylan|, and as side chains on other types of backbones, such as |FRAME: Xyloglucan xyloglucan| and |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan xylogalacturonan|. D-Mannose is also very abundant, and occurs as the polymer |FRAME: 1-4-Mannan mannan| or in combination with D-glucose or D-galactose as |FRAME: Glucomannans glucomannans|, |FRAME: Galactomannans galactomannan|, or |FRAME: Galactoglucomannans galactoglucomannan|. Arabinose is common as well, either in the form of |FRAME: Arabinans "L-arabinan"| or in the form of side chains on other polysaccharides. Other sugars common in hemicellulose include |FRAME: Galactose galactose|, |FRAME: Rhamnose rhamnose|, |FRAME: Galacturonate galacturonate| and |FRAME: Mannuronate mannuronate|. Hemicellulose consists of shorter chains than cellulose, typically 500 - 3,000 sugar units, and is usually branched.

Comment: Iron-sulfur centers consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential. In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression 16466637. [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters feature four iron ions and four sulfide ions placed at the vertices of a cubane-type structure. The Fe centers are typically further coordinated by cysteinyl ligands. Two main types of [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters are low-potential (bacterial-type) clusters and high-potential (HiPIP) clusters. The bacterial clusters shift between the oxidation states +1 and +2, while the HiPIP clusters shift between the oxidation states +2 and +3. In some enzymes the [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters bind substrates and are thus classified as enzyme cofactors. For example, in radical SAM enzymes the cluster binds and reduces S-adenosylmethionine, generating a radical that interacts with the enzyme's substrate. In a few cases, as in |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.8|, the cluster serves as the source of sulfur atoms for a sulfuration reaction 29051382.

The ferulate residues can form cross links between adjacent arabinoxylan molecules, forming |FRAME: Feraxan|. |FRAME: Arabinoxylan Arabinoxylans| are found in both the primary and secondary cell walls of plants, including woods and cereal grains, and are a component of |FRAME: Hemicelluloses|, the second most abundant renewable polysaccharide after cellulose. Compound.name: a neomycin
Comment: Neomycins are a family of broad-spectrum highly toxic antibiotics produced by |FRAME: TAX-1906|. They were discovered in 1949 by Waksman and Lechevalier (Waksman later received the 1951 Nobel Prize in Physiology and medicine) 17782716. Neomycin usually exists as a complex composed of two stereoisomers, |FRAME: CPD-14142| and |FRAME: CPD-14141|, which are the two active components. A third component, |FRAME: CPD-14137 "neomycin A"|, which is a degradation product, is present in small quantities. Neomycin was originally used as a treatment for tuberculosis, but serious side effects soon became apparent, including ototoxicity 8170691, which sometimes developed to complete loss of hearing, and nephrotoxicity. Thus systemic use of neomycin is limited, and the most common mode of use is via topical application 6224608.

Compound.name: a capsular polysaccharide
Comment: Polysaccharide capsules are ubiquitous structures found on the cell surface of a broad range of bacterial species. They are thick, mucous-like, layers of polysaccharides that form a cap around the bacterial surface.They are an important factor in the virulence of many animal and plant pathogens, where they protect the bacteria from opsonophagocytosis and complement-mediated killing by the host. Capsular polysaccharides can be linear or branched and consist of regularly repeating subunits of one to six monosaccharides. They have molecular weights on the order of 100-2000 kDa, and are linked to the cell surface of the bacterium via covalent attachments to phospholipids, lipid-A molecules, or peptidoglycan. The composition allows for a remarkable variability - over 80 different capsular polysaccharides (also known as K antigens) have been described for |FRAME: TAX-562| alone. Capsular polysaccharides are highly hydrated, and consist of over 95% water. Biosynthesis and assembly of capsular polysaccharides is a complex process. In Gram-negative bacteria the activated precursors (nucleotide monophospho and diphospho sugars) are assembled in the cytoplasm into the nascent polysaccharide by enzymes associated with the inner membrane, and while attached to the membrane by an undecaprenyl membrane anchor. A dedicated translocation pathway moves the nascent polymer through the periplasm and across the outer membrane to the cell surface, where it is removed from the membrane anchor and attached to the core oligosacchride of lipid A.

They are laid out in the cell wall at a high density and can constitute up to 50% of the algae dry mass. The basic units of |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenans| are repeats of alternating alpha-1,3 linked D-galactose and beta-1,4-linked D-galactose units, which are often substituted by sulfate. Carrageenans are classified according to the number and the position of sulfated ester 1367970. In |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units are modified by having a 3,6-anhydro bridge. These bridges, which form a double helix during aggregation, are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds. Despite this distinction, carrageenoses are often referred to as carrageenans. The three most industrially exploited carrageenans, namely, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan|, are distinguished by the presence of one, two or three ester-sulfate groups per repeating disaccharide unit respectively. |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan| is sulfated only at position 4 of the beta-1,4 linked D-galactose units.

Compound.name: a lipid A
Comment: Lipid A is a lipid component of the |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides "lipopolysaccharides"| (LPS) of Gram-negative bacteria. Its hydrophobic nature allows it to anchor the LPS to the outer membrane. Lipid A consists of two glucosamine units attached by a beta(1->6) linkage and decorated with four to seven acyl chains and one or two phosphate groups. Up to four acyl chains, often with a beta hydroxy group and usually 10 to 18 carbons in length, are attached directly to the glucosamine sugars at positions N-2 and O-3 (and N'-2 and O'-3, respectively), while additional acyl chains are attached to the beta hydroxy groups of some of those primary acyl chains. Phosphate groups can be attached at position O-1, O'-4, or both. Many variations are found in the structures of lipid A molecules. Further modifications are commonly observed, such as the addition or removal of phosphate groups (see |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.29|, |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.M9|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.M11|), the addition of |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-ETHANOLAMINE| (see |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.43|, |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.42|, and |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.M9|), the addition of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-4-DEOXY-L-ARABINOSE| units (see |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.43|), and further addition or removal of fatty acyl units (see |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.251| and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.77|). Many bacterial species produce lipid A molecules that contain |FRAME: CPD-24440| (see |FRAME: PWY-8273|). Since the fully acylated lipid A is assembled only when attached to the core oligosaccharide, a "stand alone" lipid A, as depicted here, does not occur naturally.

Compound.name: a chlorophyll

Chlorophyll absorbs light strongly in the blue and red spectra and has a strong green color. Chlorophylls play a crucial role in photosynthesis, both in the antennae and in the reaction centers. By far most of the chlorophylls are found in the antennae, where they absorb light and transfer that light energy by resonance energy transfer to the reaction center. Some of the cholorophylls (known as P700 and P680) are part of the photosystems reaction centers, where they perform the charge separation reaction, sending electrons to a transfer chain that ultimately results in the reduction of |FRAME: NADP| to |FRAME: NADPH|.

Comment: Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are isoprenoid quinones of the naphthalene series, and are constituents of bacterial plasma membranes, where they play important roles in electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation. Menaquinones are the most widespread respiratory quinones in biological systems Fujimoto12. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are named MK- n or DMK- n , respectively, where the n refers to the number of prenyl units present in the side chain. The most common length of the side chain in bacteria is 8, although minor amounts of MK-1 through MK-14 have been found 7022156. Many bacteria and archaea have |FRAME: Dihydromenaquinones "dehydrogenated menaquinones"|, which are named MK- n (H 2 ). The degree and location of dehydrogenation depends on the species. Some organisms have menaquinones with modifications of the head group, for example |FRAME: TAX-2302| possess both |FRAME: CPD-15875 thermoplasmaquinones| (TPQ), which contains an extra methyl group, and |FRAME: CPD-15876 methionaquinones| (MTK), which contains a methylthio group 11157962. Menaquinones are also known as vitamin K 2 . Vitamin K is a name given to a group of derivatives of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone that are required by mammals for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, mostly involved in blood coagulation. These compounds, while essential for mammals, are not synthesized by them, and are thus considered vitamins. The natural forms of the vitamin are vitamin K 1 (|FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE|) and vitamin K 2 (|FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinone"|). Since menaquinones produced by different organisms have different tail lengths there are many variations of vitamin K 2 , usually specified based on the number of carbons in their tails, such as in Vitamin K 2 (45). The reduced form of menaquinone is called |FRAME: Menaquinols|.

It was found in high amounts on the surface of human pancreatic, colon and gastric cancer cell lines |CITS: [7142214][6188455]| and in human adenocarcinomas of the colon, stomach, pancreas and gall-bladder |CITS: [94699][6751528][2910493]|. The expression of the antigen has been linked to tumor progression. A gradual increase in SLe a was found in colon and rectum during neoplastic transformation and progression 2863413, and its presence was restricted to tumorigenic and invasive human urothelial cell lines 8900435. The antigen is responsible for adhesion of colon, pancreas, urinary bladder and gastric cancer cells to endothelium via its interaction with selectin E |CITS: [1716885][7687590][7678075][8900435][9578490]|. The expression level of the SLe a antigen is used as a prognostic factor for colorectal carcinoma, and is associated with high incidence of recurrence and the length of survival time |CITS: [8273774][7697593][9303355]|.

Compound.name: compound 0
Comment: |FRAME: Compound-0 "Compound 0"|, |FRAME: Compound-I|, and |FRAME: Compound-II| are the names given to intermediate states of the heme-iron center that is formed at the active sites of cytochrome P-450 enzymes and peroxidases during catalysis. I. Cytochrome P-450 In cytochrome P-450 the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a cysteine thiolate ligand. At its rest state, the iron is found at a low-spin ferric state (III valency). At this state the iron also binds a water molecule as a sixth ligand at the distal axial coordination position. Binding of a substrate to the low-spin ferric enzyme leads to displacement of the water as the sixth ligand and a high spin shift. The substrate-bound complex has a greater reduction potential and more easily accepts a single electron from the redox partner, which can be either |FRAME: EC-1.6.2.4 "a cytochrome P450 reductase"|, |FRAME: Ferredoxins|, or |FRAME: Cytochromes-b5|). After the first reduction, the heme iron binds oxygen, forming an oxy-heme complex. The oxygen is bound at the distal axial coordination position, from which the water molecule has been displaced. Following the transfer of the second electron from the redox partner and two subsequent protonations, a peroxo adduct is formed, known as |FRAME: Compound-0|. Next, the O-O bond is cleaved heterolytically, releasing a water molecule and leaving behind an oxygen atom with only six valence electrons. This highly active oxene oxygen removes one electron from the iron and one from the porphyrin, oxidizing the iron to the unusual valency of IV (ferryl iron) and generating an additional oxidizing equivalent that is delocalized over the porphyrin and thiolate ligands. This ferryl/porphyrin radical cation complex is known as |FRAME: Compound-I| 21071661. When the substrate nears the active site, |FRAME: Compound-I| abstracts an electron from it, converting the substrate into a radical and becoming a protonated non-radical ferryl compound known as |FRAME: Compound-II|. At this point the substrate radical reacts with the oxygen of |FRAME: Compound-II|, forming a new carbon oxygen bond. The product is released, and the iron returns to a valency of III (compound III) OrtizdeMontellano15. II. preoxidases In peroxidases the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a histidine residue. |FRAME: Compound-I "Compound I"| is produced when the heme iron is oxidized by |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. A single one-electron reduction step of |FRAME: Compound-I| from an electron donor substrate yields |FRAME: Compound-II|, followed by a second one-electron transfer that returns the enzyme to the ferric oxidation state, thus completing the catalytic cycle. Each electron transfer event converts a substrate molecule to a radical cation, forming two such radicals during a catalytic cycle. In the presence of high concentrations of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and the absence of a reducing substrate, |FRAME: Compound-II| can be oxidized to |FRAME: Compound-III|, a catalytically inactive form of the enzyme. |FRAME: Compound-III "Compound III"| is converted back to the resting state by spontaneous autoxidation or by oxidation with two molecules of the substrate radical cation 18581264.

The most common repeating unit, which makes up around 50% of the total disaccharide units in heparan sulfate, is composed of |FRAME: CPD-12521| linked to |FRAME: CPD-12541|. This alternative unit, which is a substrate for heparanase, consists of |FRAME: CPD-12521| linked to |FRAME: N6-O-disulfo-D-glucosamine| 20181948.

Compound.name: a glucuronoxylan oligosaccharide
Comment: |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans Glucuronoxylans| are linear polymers of beta-D-xylopyranosyl units linked by (1->4) glycosidic bonds, with many of the xylose units substituted with (1->2)- and/or (1->3)-linked glucuronate residues. Many of the D-glucuronosyl units are methylated at position 4. Angiosperm (hardwood) glucuronoxylans also have a high rate of substitution (70-80%) by acetyl groups, at position 2 and/or 3 of the beta-D-xylopyranosyl, conferring on the xylan its partial solubility in water. Glucuronoxylan oligosaccharides are formed from glucuronoxylan by the action of glucuronoxylanase enzymes (|FRAME: 3.2.1.136-RXN "EC 3.2.1.136"|)

Compound.name: a sphingolipid

They are named for the mythological Sphinx because at the time (1884) their function was enigmatic Thudichum84. The sphingosine backbone (often referred to as the |FRAME: Sphingoids "sphingoid base"|) is amide-linked to an acyl group, such as a fatty acid, and is often also O -linked to a charged head group such as ethanolamine, serine, or choline. There are three main types of sphingolipids: |FRAME: Ceramides ceramides|, |FRAME: Sphingomyelins sphingomyelins|, and |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids glycosphingolipids|. Ceramides are the most simple sphingolipids, composed of only the sphingoid base and a fatty acid. Sphingomyelins are composed of a ceramide bound to a charged head group, usually |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE|. Glycosphingolipids are composed of a ceramide with attached mono- or oligosaccharide moieties. Mammals usually produce |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE|-containing |FRAME: Sphingomyelins sphingomyelins|, while plants and fungi usually produce glycosphingolipids with inositol as the head group.

Compound.name: a capsaicinoid
Comment: The pungency of chili or hot peppers comes from phenolic alkaloids called |FRAME: Capsaicinoids capsaicinoids|. These compounds are exclusively produced in fruits of plants belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-4071| genus. A quarter of the world population consumes hot peppers in some form daily 16938870. Structurally capsaicinoids consist of a common aromatic moiety, |FRAME: CPD-9327|, modified by a short chain fatty acid that may have variable length and different degrees of saturation Curry99. The accumulation of |FRAME: Capsaicinoids capsaicinoids| is strictly correlated with developmental stages of the fruit and usually spans the ripening stages after fruit size increase has ceased SUKRASNO93. The capsaicinoids are localized in the epidermal cells of the fruit placenta 12810854. Pungency differs considerably in species ranging from very hot to sweet peppers and has a positive correlation with the level of capsaicinoids biosynthetic gene expression 12810854. |FRAME: CAPSAICIN Capsaicin| and |FRAME: CPD-9185| are the most common types. Other naturally occurring capsaicinoids include |FRAME: CPD-9182|, |FRAME: CPD-9333|, |FRAME: CPD-9331|, |FRAME: CPD-9181|, and |FRAME: CPD-9330|, which differ in the fatty acid chain length (n=7-10) and the presence and/or position of a double bond Curry99.

All available positions, O2, O3, and O6, can be modified. It is often used as its sodium salt, sodium carboxymethyl cellulose. Unlike unmodified cellulose, carboxymethylcellulose is soluble in water. CMC is used in food science as a viscosity modifier or thickener, and to stabilize emulsions in various products including ice cream. It is also a constituent of many non-food products, such as K-Y Jelly, toothpaste, laxatives, diet pills, water-based paints, detergents, textile sizing and various paper products.

Compound.name: cob(I)alamin-[methionine synthase]
Comment: |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13| is a vitamin B12-dependent zinc metalloenzyme that catalyzes the transfer of a methyl group from |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N| to homocysteine. Methionine synthase is one of two eukaryotic enzymes that require a cobalamin prosthetic group for activity. Unlike the other enzyme (|FRAME: EC-5.4.99.2|), which requires adenosylcobalamin, the cobalamin cofactor of methionine synthase needs to be methylated. Upon the initial transfer of a cob(II)alamin cofactor from a |FRAME: CPD-20918|, it is methylated to the active methylcob(III)alamin form by |FRAME: EC-1.16.1.8|, which uses |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as the methyl donor. The methyl group is subsequently transferred to homocysteine to form methionine, leaving the cofactor briefly in a cob(I)alamin form, which is regenerated to the active methylcob(III)alamin form by a transfer of a methyl group from |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N "5-methyltetrahydrofolate"| 2407589. The enzyme becomes inactivated occasionally during its cycle by oxidation of Co(I) to Co(II). Reactivation by reductive methylation is catalysed by the enzyme itself, with S-adenosyl-L-methionine as the methyl donor and a reducing system. For the mammalian enzyme, the reducing system involves NADPH and |FRAME: EC-1.16.1.8|. In bacteria, the reducing agent is flavodoxin, and no further catalyst is needed (the flavodoxin is kept in the reduced state by NADPH and |FRAME: EC-1.18.1.2|). A histidine residue embedded in the canonical B 12 -binding DxHxxG motif in methionine synthase serves as the lower axial ligand to the cobalt, which is bound in the "base-off/His-on" state 7992050.

Comment: LysW is an amino-group-carrier protein used by many archaeal species for the synthesis of the amino acid |FRAME: LYS|. The amino group of |FRAME: CPD-468|, an intermediate in the |FRAME: PWY-3081 "archaeal L-lysine biosynthetic pathway"| (which is also found in the hyperthermophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-274|), is covalently linked to the gamma-carboxyl group of the last C-terminal residue of LysW (Glu54 in |FRAME: TAX-274|) by a dedicated enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-5207| gene. It has been shown that in some species, such as members of the |FRAME: TAX-2284| genus 23434852 and |FRAME: TAX-311400| 27566549 LysW is also used as a carrier protein for |FRAME: GLT| during the |FRAME: PWY-7400 "biosynthesis of L-arginine"|.

Compound.name: compound I
Comment: |FRAME: Compound-0 "Compound 0"|, |FRAME: Compound-I|, and |FRAME: Compound-II| are the names given to intermediate states of the heme-iron center that is formed at the active sites of cytochrome P-450 enzymes and peroxidases during catalysis. I. Cytochrome P-450 In |FRAME: Cytochrome-P450 "cytochrome P-450"| the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a cysteine thiolate ligand. At its rest state, the iron is found at a low-spin ferric state (III valency). At this state the iron also binds a water molecule as a sixth ligand at the distal axial coordination position. Binding of a substrate to the low-spin ferric enzyme leads to displacement of the water as the sixth ligand and a high spin shift. The substrate-bound complex has a greater reduction potential and more easily accepts a single electron from the redox partner, which can be either |FRAME: EC-1.6.2.4 "a cytochrome P450 reductase"|, |FRAME: Ferredoxins|, or |FRAME: Cytochromes-b5|). After the first reduction, the heme iron binds oxygen, forming an oxy-heme complex. The oxygen is bound at the distal axial coordination position, from which the water molecule has been displaced. Following the transfer of the second electron from the redox partner and two subsequent protonations, a peroxo adduct is formed, known as |FRAME: Compound-0|. Next, the O-O bond is cleaved heterolytically, releasing a water molecule and leaving behind an oxygen atom with only six valence electrons. This highly active oxene oxygen removes one electron from the iron and one from the porphyrin, oxidizing the iron to the unusual valency of IV (ferryl iron) and generating an additional oxidizing equivalent that is delocalized over the porphyrin and thiolate ligands. This ferryl/porphyrin radical cation complex is known as |FRAME: Compound-I| 21071661. When the substrate nears the active site, |FRAME: Compound-I| abstracts an electron from it, converting the substrate into a radical and becoming a protonated non-radical ferryl compound known as |FRAME: Compound-II|. At this point the substrate radical reacts with the oxygen of |FRAME: Compound-II|, forming a new carbon oxygen bond. The product is released, and the iron returns to a valency of III (compound III) OrtizdeMontellano15. II. preoxidases In peroxidases the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a histidine residue. |FRAME: Compound-I "Compound I"| is produced when the heme iron is oxidized by |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. A single one-electron reduction step of |FRAME: Compound-I| from an electron donor substrate yields |FRAME: Compound-II|, followed by a second one-electron transfer that returns the enzyme to the ferric oxidation state, thus completing the catalytic cycle. Each electron transfer event converts a substrate molecule to a radical cation, forming two such radicals during a catalytic cycle. In the presence of high concentrations of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and the absence of a reducing substrate, |FRAME: Compound-II| can be oxidized to |FRAME: Compound-III|, a catalytically inactive form of the enzyme. |FRAME: Compound-III "Compound III"| is converted back to the resting state by spontaneous autoxidation or by oxidation with two molecules of the substrate radical cation 18581264.

The terms ubiquinone/ubiquinol refer to the oxidized/reduced forms, and are often used interchangeably. The forms are readily interconvertable. Ubiquinone is also known as coenzyme Q, or just Q. The names are often followed by the number of the prenoid units in the side chain (e.g. Q-8), or the number of carbons in the chain. For example, the name Q-8 may be substituted with ubiquinone(40). Since these carbons occur in repeating units of five, these number are multiples of 5.

Compound.name: an N 10 -formyltetrahydrofolate
Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of various cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551. This class stands for 10-formyltetrahydrofolates with an unspecified number of glutamate residues.

However, in certain filamentous fungi galactofuranose (Gal f ) is found in galactomannan instead of galactopyranose. The galactomannan attached to N -glycans in |FRAME: TAX-746128| is composed of a linear mannan core comprising |FRAME: CPD-20116 "alpha-(1-2)-linked mannotetraose"| repeating units attached to each other via alpha-(1-6) linkages and decorated by side chains of beta-(1-5)-galactofuranose units, which are linked to the C2 position of the non-reducing mannose residue in each mannotetraose unit 7960122. The length of the side chains depends on growth conditions. Cells grown in YPD medium produced galactomannan with side chain consisting an average of 3-4 units of galactofuranose |CITS: [7960122][25187160]|, while cells grown in YNB medium incorporated on average 10 Gal f units that may contain one beta-(1,6) linkage midchain 25187160. It should be noted that a different form of galactomannan containing galactofuranose resides is found in O -glycans produced by this organism, in which the mannan core is much shorter, consisting of only one to two mannosyl residues 25187160.

Compound.name: a polyisoprenyl-teichoic acid
Comment: Teichoic acids were first reported in 1958 Armstrong58, after being discovered serendipitously as "contaminants" in bacterial extracts from |FRAME: TAX-1590| 2662967. As they make up a significant portion of the cell walls (about 60% in |FRAME: TAX-1423|) 13684313, they were named based on the Greek word teikhos, which means a fortification wall. The teichoic acids are found in the cell walls of a wide range of Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [5411858][2496299]|. There are two main types of teichoic acids: the lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are anchored to the plasma membrane and extend from the cell surface into the peptidoglycan layer 406922, and the wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently attached to peptidoglycan and extend through and beyond the cell wall. In |FRAME: TAX-224308| the main form of teichoic acid is a polymer of |FRAME: CPD-75 "poly(glycerol phosphate)"|, while in |FRAME: TAX-655816| the major variety is a polymer of |FRAME: CPD-19310 "poly(ribitol phosphate)"| 13684313. In both cases, the repeating units are joined together by phosphodiester linkages, and are anchored via 2-3 glycerol phosphate units to a N -acetyl-beta-D-mannosaminyl-(1->4)- N -acetyl-alpha-D-glucosamine disaccharide. The glycerol and ribitol units of the polysaccharides are modified with D-alanine esters and/or monosaccharides such as glucose or N -acetylglucosamine |CITS: [13684313][4321415]|. It should be noted that strain 168 also possesses a |FRAME: CPD-19345 "minor form of wall teichoic acid"| that is comprised of poly(glucosyl N -acetylgalactosamine 1-phosphate) 4202940). Teichoic acids serve several roles in the cell. They serve as reservoirs of phosphates which can be mobilized when phosphate becomes limiting 104966. Being anionic, they are scavengers of cations (in particular Mg 2+ ), and may create a pH gradient across the wall by sequestering the protons expelled through the cytoplasmic membrane 8396121. In addition, lipoteichoic acids are the main source of the hydrophobicity of the cell envelope 6337099, and may contribute to its adhesiveness. Teichoic acids are also immunogenic, and can be considered the Gram-positive equivalent of the Gram-negative lipopolysaccharides 46620.

Compound.name: a 2-demethylmenaquinone
Comment: Menaquinols are the reduced form of |FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinones"|. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are isoprenoid quinones of the naphthalene series, and are constituents of bacterial plasma membranes, where they play important roles in electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are named MK- n or DMK- n , respectively, where the n refers to the number of prenyl units present in the side chain. The most common length of the side chain in bacteria is 8, although minor amounts of MK-1 through MK-14 have been found 7022156. Menaquinones are also known as vitamin K 2 . Vitamin K is a name given to a group of derivatives of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone that are required by mammals for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, mostly involved in blood coagulation. These compounds, while essential for mammals, are not synthesized by them, and are thus considered vitamins. The natural forms of the vitamin are vitamin K 1 (|FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE|) and vitamin K 2 (|FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinone"|). Since menaquinones produced by different organisms have different tail lenghts there are many variations of vitamin K 2 , usually specified based on the number of carbons in their tails, such as in Vitamin K 2 (45).

Unlike cosubstrates, the cofactors are restored to their original state at the end of the catalytic cycle and are thus not included in the reaction equation. Cofactors can be inorganic ions (e.g. Ca 2+ ), inorganic molecules (e.g. |FRAME: FeS-Centers|) or organic molecules (e.g. |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|). Some compounds may act as cofactors for a particular enzyme and a cosubstrate for a different enzyme, depending on whether they are restored to their active state at the end of the reaction. Cofactors that are tightly bound to an enzyme have often been referred to as prosthetic groups. It should be noted that the degree of tightness required for this definition has not been defined, and that the same cofactor may bind differently to different enzymes, making this term imprecise. Thus, it is recommended not to use it. Organic cofactors that are loosely bound to the enzyme have been often referred to as coenzymes. They are produced from the common isoprene precursor |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|. The diverse carbon skeletons of diterpenes are formed through carbocation-mediated cyclization cascades catalyzed by diterpene cyclases. Diterpene cyclases are categorized into two classes, class I and class II, on the basis of their reaction mechanisms and catalytic domains.

The attachment sites of the acyl chains at the R1 (sn-1), R2 (sn-2), or R3 (sn-3) position along the glyceryl backbone may vary among class members and cannot be inferred from their order in the compound class name. Compound.name: a glycogen
Comment: Glycogen is a highly branched glucose polymer found in archaea, bacteria, and eukaryotes. It resembles plant-produced |FRAME: Starch starch| and is sometimes called "animal starch". Glycogen serves multiple functions, including energy reserve, osmotic regulation, blood glucose homeostasis, and pH maintenance. Glycogen is formed of small chains of 8 to 12 glucose molecules linked together by alpha (1->4) bonds. These small chains, also known as |FRAME: Maltodextrins maltodextrins|, are in turn linked together by alpha (1->6) bonds. The alpha-1,4 linkages make up approximately 95% of the total molecule. The alpha-1,6 branches accounts for 7–10% of the linkages and are evenly distributed within the glycogen particle. Since each chain (with the exception of the outer unbranched chains) supports two branches, glycogen particles grow spherically by adding tiers (a tier corresponds to the spherical space separating two consecutive branches from all chains located at similar distance from the center of the particle). Two structural levels of glycogen particles have been reported, which are tightly associated with their physiological functions: small quasi-spherical beta particles, as found in muscle cells, and large rosette-shaped alpha particles, as found in liver cells. The diameter of beta particles normally range from 10 to 50 nm, with an average at around 20—30 nm. The beta particles can stick together to form large alpha particles with diameters up to 300 nm |CITS: [20196533][31244022][33996916]|. Two types of alpha particles have been observed: fragile and dense particles, which comprise large and dense beta particles with long average chain length, and stable light particles, which comprise smaller, compact beta particles with short average chain length 31244022. Mathematical modelling predicts a maximal size for the beta particle beyond which further growth is impossible, as there would not be sufficient space for interaction of the chains with the catalytic sites of glycogen metabolism enzymes. The predicted upper limit is a particle consisting of 12 tiers corresponding to a 42 nm maximal diameter and including about 55,000 glucose residues. 36% of this total number rests in the outer (unbranched) shell and is thus readily accessible to glycogen catabolism without the need for debranching 12179957. Although glycogen and starch are two distinct physical states of the same type of storage polysaccharide, starch is solid semi-crystalline while glycogen particles are entirely hydrosoluble 21220783.

Compound.name: an N -linked glycoprotein

These asparagine residues are found in special sequences known as the sequon, which are composed of three consecutive amino acids that are recognized as the signal for the attachment of the N -glycan. The sequence of a sequon is either Asn-X-Ser or Asn-X-Thr, where X is any amino acid except for proline. N -glycans may be composed of N -acetyl galactosamine, galactose, neuraminic acid, N -acetylglucosamine, fructose, mannose, fucose and other monosaccharides.

Compound.name: a beta-lactam
Comment: This compound class stands for |FRAME: Lactams lactams| in which the amide bond is contained within a four-membered ring, which includes the amide nitrogen and the carbonyl carbon. beta-Lactam compounds imitate the naturally occurring |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| substrate for the group of enzymes known as penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), which cross-link the peptidoglycan in bacterial cell wall, and thus act as powerful antibiotics 6109324. Naturally occurring |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam antibiotics"| are classified into several groups according to their chemical structure: In |FRAME: Monolactams monolactams| the beta-lactam ring is not fused to another ring. This class includes compounds such as the |FRAME: Nocardicins nocardicins| 3427723 and the |FRAME: Monobactams monobactams| 3909315. In |FRAME: Penams penams| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a saturated five atom ring (a 4:5 structure). Penams contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring (for example, the |FRAME: PENICILLIN penicillins|) 6335599. Related classes include the |FRAME: Carbapenams carbapenams|, which contain a carbon atom in that position 12890666, and the |FRAME: Clavams oxopenams| (also known as clavams), which contain an oxygen atom at that position (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|) 3304182. |FRAME: Penems Penems| are molecues similar to penams in which the five atom ring is unsaturated at positions 2-3. Similarly, penems contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring, while |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| contains a carbon atom in that position 16413506. In |FRAME: Cephams cephams| and |FRAME: Cephems cephems| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a six-atom ring (a 4:6 strcuture) that contains a sulfur atom at position 1. In cephams the ring is saturated, while cephems have an unsaturated bond at positions 3-4 |CITS: [1164170][12722308]|. 1-Oxocephams/1-oxacephems conain an oxygen atom at position 1 |CITS: [11671696][11078187]|.

Compound.name: a phenylpropanoid
Comment: The phenylpropanoids are a large family of compounds, mostly found in plants, that are synthesized from |FRAME: PHE| and, to a lesser extent, |FRAME: TYR|. The pathway that starts from |FRAME: PHE| forms |FRAME: COUMARATE| as a main intermediate. The name "phenylpropanoid" is derived from this compound, which consists of an aromatic phenyl group and a propene tail. Further processing results in the biosynthesis of many types of compounds, including |FRAME: Lignols monolignols| (precursors to |FRAME: Lignins lignin| and lignocellulose), |FRAME: Flavonoids flavonoids|, |FRAME: Coumarins coumarins|, |FRAME: Stilbenoids stilbenoids|, and phenolic acids. Phenylpropanoids are found throughout the plant kingdom, where they serve as essential components of a number of structural polymers, provide protection from ultraviolet light, defend against herbivores and pathogens, and also mediate plant-pollinator interactions as floral pigments and scent compounds.

Compound.name: a fructooligosaccharide
Comment: Fructooligosaccharides (FOS), sometimes called oligofructose or oligofructan, are a class of oligosaccharides used as an artificial or alternative sweetener. A common source of FOS is the hydrolysis of |FRAME: Inulin inulin| by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.7|, which results in two types of FOS: either oligosaccharides consisting solely of fructose [(beta-D-Fru f -(2->1)-beta-D-Fru f )] n (e.g. |FRAME: INULOBIOSE|, |FRAME: CPD-24815|, and |FRAME: CPD-24816|), or oligosaccharides that terminate with glucose [(beta-D-Fru f -(2->1)-beta-D-Fru f )] n -(21)-alpha-D-Glc p (e.g. |FRAME: 1-KESTOTRIOSE|, |FRAME: NYSTOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-24817|). The second mechanism that produces FOS is the transfructosylation action of |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.26|, on |FRAME: SUCROSE|, which results in FOS of the general formula G(F n ) that can contain linkages other than beta(1->2) 24528719. FOS exhibit sweetness levels between 30 and 50 percent of sugar, and are used as alternative sweeteners. They resist hydrolysis by salivary and intestinal digestive enzymes, but are fermented in the colon by anaerobic bacteria. They are considered probiotics |CITS: [10075343][14747679][19152479]| and may stimulate the growth of beneficial bacteria such as Bifidobacteria species 19152479.

Compound.name: an apo -["base-off/His-on" B12-enzyme]

In the carbon skeleton mutases and aminomutases an |FRAME: HIS| residue, part of a conserved DxHxxG motif from the protein 1397267, replaces the dimethylbenzimidazole tail as the lower ligand to cobalt, which is instead extended down into the core of the protein. This mode of binding has been termed "base-off/His-on"" |CITS: [Padmakumar95a][8805541]|. In contrast, in the eliminases the adenosylcobalamin is bound with the dimethylbenzimidazole base coordinated to cobalt, as it is in free solution. This mode is known as "dmb-on" |CITS: [9537996][10496987]|. Why different proteins use different binding mode of their adenosylcobalamin cofactor remains unclear 22516318.

Common |FRAME: Ribonucleosides ribonucleosides| include |FRAME: CYTIDINE|, |FRAME: URIDINE|, |FRAME: ADENOSINE|, |FRAME: GUANOSINE| and |FRAME: INOSINE|. Examples of |FRAME: Deoxy-Ribonucleosides deoxyribonucleosides| include |FRAME: THYMIDINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYADENOSINE|. When nucleosides are phosphorylated on the sugar's primary alcohol group, the resulting phosphonucleosides are called |FRAME: Nucleotides nucleotides|.

Compound.name: a megalomicin
Comment: The megalomicins, which were discovered in 1968 |CITS:[5735370][5810991]|, are a family of related macrolide antibiotics produced by the soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-47868|. Chitosan is mostly produced commercially by deacetylation of |FRAME: CHITIN| , which is the structural element in the exoskeleton of crustaceans. The most popular technique for obtaining chitosan is alkaline deacetylation of chitin: this involves boiling chitin in concentrated alkali (50% w/v) for several hours. This process also yields chitosan with a degree of acetylation between 20-30%. However, in such a chitosan, unlike the naturally occurring chitosan, the acetyl groups are uniformly distributed along the polymer chain. Completely de-acetylated forms of chitosan do not exist naturally, but can be synthesized by special chemical treatment.

Compound.name: a cardenolide glycoside
Comment: Cardiac glycosides are plant-made compounds (mostly by members of the |FRAME: TAX-4163| genus, or Foxgloves) that have beneficial effects over patients with cardiac failure. The treatment of congestive heart failure (dropsy), among other ailments like tuberculosis, by the use of Foxglove is mentioned in writings as early as 1250 A. D., when the Welsh Physicians of Myddva collected foxglove as one of their many herbs and included it in their remedies. 28561136. The cardiac glycosides are composed of two structural features: a sugar moiety that may contain one or more saccharides, and a steroid aglycone. Cardiac glycosides having a terminal glucose are called primary glycosides whereas those lacking such a sugar are termed secondary glycosides. There are two classes of cardiac glycosides differing by the group attached at the 17-position of the aglycone: the |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolides"|, which have a five-membered unsaturated lactone ring (but-2-en-4-olide ring) and the |FRAME: Bufadienolide-Glycosides bufadienolides|, which have a six membered doubly unsaturated lactone ring (penta-2,4-dien-5-olide ring). The steroid nucleus of the cardiac glycosides have a unique configuration: rings A/B and C/D are cis - fused while rings B/C are trans - fused. The nucleus has beta configured hydroxyls at the positions C-3 and C-14, and many compounds have additional hydroxyl groups at positions 12 and 16. The sugars found in the glycoside moiety range from common hexoses and pentoses (such as |FRAME: D-Glucose|, |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-Xylose|) to very uncommon sugars, some of which have only been found in cardiac glycosides (e.g. |FRAME: D-quinovopyranose|, |FRAME: CPD-22597|, |FRAME: D-Digitoxose|, |FRAME: CPD-22572|, |FRAME: D-Olivose|, and |FRAME: D-Fucoses|). While the mechanism whereby cardiac glycosides cause a positive inotropic effect and electrophysiologic changes of the hurt is still not completely clear, the most widely accepted mechanism involves the ability of cardiac glycosides to inhibit the membrane bound Na+/K+-ATPase pump responsible for Na+/K+ exchange KAUTE08.

Comment: Green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-191412|) and green flimentous bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1106|) contain chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. Green sulfur bacteria can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph, up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight Overmann92. Chlorosomes contain about 1,500 bacteriochlorophyll molecules per reaction center. They are filled with 10 30 rod-shaped elements which are oriented parallel to the long axis of the chlorosomes and have a diameter of 10 nm. Each rod consists of a tubular bilayer formed by self-organization of the antenna bacteriochlorophyll molecules. Unlike all other known photosynthetic antenna, in which the chlorophyll molecules are bound to proteins, chlorosomes do not contain accessory proteins. The chlorosomal bacteriochlorophyll pigments are able to self-aggregate due to their unique chemical characteristics. The bacteriochlorophylls found in chlorosomes are either |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "|, depending on the species. In addition, all of these bacteriochlorophylls lack C-13 2 -methylcarboxyl side chains, which are found in all other (bacterio)chlorophylls but would interfere with the ability to form aggregates 16245042. Despite of their names, |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| and |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "| are actually chlorins rather than bacteriochlorins. In general, pimgents produced by cultures grown at lower light intensities are more highly methylated at the C-8 2 position than pigments produced by cells of the same organism grown at higher light intensities. Different methylation states result in different aggregation properties and light absorbance of the chlorosome, and thus methylation is used as an adaptation to altering envireonmental conditions. Most of the green sulfur bacteria growing in stratified lakes contain CPD-9093, and species containing |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "| are rarely found vanGemerden95.

Compound.name: a carotenoid
Comment: |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A. Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see 15012246). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis. Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Although biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis from |FRAME: CPD1F-114| have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated, details of all of the enzyme reactions involved in these pathways remain to be determined (as in |CITS: [20802040] [17008032] [11511870] [11432736]|). Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|. Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses 20582313.

Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of various cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551.
